BUG: LSAN Detected Memory Leaks

### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example


Invoke meson via `pip install -ve . --no-build-isolation --config-settings=builddir="asan" --config-settings=setup-args="-Db_sanitize=address"`


Also create an LSAN "suppression file" with these contents:

```
leak:unicode_decode_utf8
leak:PyObject_Malloc
```

Name that file and provide it via an *absolute path* to the below command:

`LSAN_OPTIONS=suppressions=<absolute_path_to_suppression_file> LD_PRELOAD=$(gcc -print-file-name=libasan.so)  python -m pytest pandas/tests/io/json/`


### Issue Description

You have to sift through a lot, but ASAN detects direct leaks in our codebase from at least the following locations (just running JSON test suite above):

I have a hunch that LSAN may be misreporting bytes that Cython releases in any `__dealloc__` calls when they are constructed via pytest parameters. Haven't verified that is the case for these in particular, but something worth further investigation


query:
DOC: read_csv "quoting" type is malformed

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html > Parameters > quoting

### Documentation problem

The type information bleeds into the description:

> **quoting : {0 or csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, 1 or csv.QUOTE_ALL,**
> 2 or csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC, 3 or csv.QUOTE_NONE}, default csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL Control field quoting behavior per `csv.QUOTE_*` constants. Default is `csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL` (i.e., 0) which implies that only fields containing special characters are quoted (e.g., characters defined in `quotechar`, `delimiter`, or `lineterminator`.

### Suggested fix for documentation

It should look like this:

> **quoting : {0 or csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, 1 or csv.QUOTE_ALL, 2 or csv.QUOTE_NONNUMERIC, 3 or csv.QUOTE_NONE}, default csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL**
> Control field quoting behavior per `csv.QUOTE_*` constants. Default is `csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL` (i.e., 0) which implies that only fields containing special characters are quoted (e.g., characters defined in `quotechar`, `delimiter`, or `lineterminator`.

PERF: String column serialization in Interchange protocol is slow

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example


### Problem Description
Currently, when serializing string columns to a byte buffer in the DataFrame Interchange Protocol (`pandas/core/interchange/column.py`), pandas uses a slow element-wise Python loop:

```python
for obj in buf:
    if isinstance(obj, str):
        b.extend(obj.encode(encoding="utf-8"))
```

For large DataFrames ($100k+$ or $1M+$ rows), this loop is highly inefficient because:
1. It calls `.encode("utf-8")` once for every single string element inside the Python interpreter.
2. It uses `bytearray.extend()` iteratively, introducing overhead.
3. The check `isinstance(obj, str)` is run iteratively in Python.

### Proposed Optimization
We can leverage NumPy to filter nulls/invalid elements in C-space and then perform a single C-optimized join and a single vectorized `.encode()` call:

```python
# Drop null values to avoid joining None/NaN
b = "".join(buf[pd.notna(buf)]).encode(encoding="utf-8")
```

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked the original loop logic vs. the optimized NumPy mask & join approach on array sizes with 5% missing values:

| Size (Strings) | Original Loop | Optimized Python | Speedup Factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **10,000** | 0.00530s | 0.00227s | **2.34x** |
| **100,000** | 0.06940s | 0.02344s | **2.96x** |
| **1,000,000** | 0.22295s | 0.10143s | **2.20x** |

PERF: High overhead in stack frame warning inspections (find_stack_level)

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

### Problem Description
Whenever pandas raises a warning, it invokes `find_stack_level()` to trace the call stack and identify the calling context outside of pandas. Currently, this function walks the stack frames and calls `inspect.getfile(frame)` inside a loop:

```python
while frame:
    filename = inspect.getfile(frame)
    if filename.startswith(pkg_dir) and not filename.startswith(test_dir):
        frame = frame.f_back
        n += 1
```

For workloads that emit multiple warnings (or libraries relying heavily on pandas warnings), this function is highly inefficient because:
1. `inspect.getfile(frame)` is slow as it does lookup caching, module parsing, and absolute path validation inside the interpreter loop.
2. It repeatedly imports `pandas` and resolves `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths on *every* warning invocation.

### Proposed Optimization
1. Cache the `pkg_dir` and `test_dir` paths globally at the module level.
2. Retrieve the filename directly via `frame.f_code.co_filename` instead of calling `inspect.getfile(frame)`.

### Performance Benchmarks
We benchmarked 500,000 runs of the original stack inspection vs. the optimized caching and `co_filename` check on a local environment:

| Implementation | 500,000 runs | Overhead per call |
|---|---|---|
| **Original (`master`)** | 3.67 seconds | ~7.33 microseconds |
| **Optimized** | 0.19 seconds | ~0.38 microseconds |

This yields a **~19x speedup** (95% reduction in call overhead).

So I have looked into the code and here are the problems i found:
1. In df.to_hdf, if you don't set complevel, it wouldn't get compressed even complib is explicitly set.
2. The API of HDFStore is kinda confusing as you can set complevel/complib in two places - when constructing the HDFStore instance and when calling put/append. And the latter take priority if complib is explicitly set.
For example,
```py
with HDFStore(tmpfile, "w", complevel=5, complib='bzip2') as store:
    store.put(gname, df, format='t')
```
would result in bzip2(5), whereas
```py
with HDFStore(tmpfile, "w", complevel=5, complib='bzip2') as store:
    store.put(gname, df, format='t', complevel=2, complib='zlib')
```
would result in zlib(2)
only specify ```complib='zlib'``` in ```put``` would result in zlib(5) and
only specify ```complevel=2``` in ```put``` would result in bzip2(5) (complib is not explicitly set in store.put)
3. In HDFStore, there is a check which only accept table format if compressing. But the check is not working.
4. With fixed format, the file size of the "compressed" version is bigger than that of no compress. (maybe that's why we have no3)

So my suggestions are
- For (1), we can add to the doc to address this issue, or having a default complevel value if complib is explicitly set.
- Regarding the HDFStore, for a quick fix, we could modify so that  the args in put/append method always take priority over those stored in self. In the long run, we should only have complevel, complib in one place.

But imo, doing just the former (and maybe fix the check) would already resolves this issue. The latter one deserve its own issue

#### Problem description

In `read_hdf`, if the `store.select()` call throws either a `ValueError`, a `TypeError` or a `KeyError` then the store is closed.

reopening in write mode`.

BUG: ExcelFile.parse sets sheet.max_row and sheet.max_column to None

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
# /// script
# dependencies = [
#     "openpyxl",
#     "pandas",
# ]
# ///
import pandas as pd

# Assuming "some_file.xlsx" exists and contains a sheet "Sheet1" with
# some data, for example cell A1="A Header" and cell A2=1234

with pd.ExcelFile("some_file.xlsx") as excel_file:
    ws = excel_file.book["Sheet1"]

    dim_before = (ws.max_row, ws.max_column)
    print(f"Dimensions of Sheet1: {dim_before=}")

    df = excel_file.parse(sheet_name=ws.title)

    dim_after = (ws.max_row, ws.max_column)

    print(f"Dimensions of Sheet1: {dim_after=}")

assert dim_before == dim_after  # assert fails!

# Expect same values
# But we get dim_before=(2, 1) or whatever is in the file
# and dim_after=(None, None) - unexpectedly dimensions are now None
```

### Issue Description

When using Pandas to read tables from Excel worksheets, the `parse` function messes with the internal dimension variables - it sets max_row and max_column to None.

This is caused by `pandas/io/excel/_openpyxl.py` lines 610 + 611 (the last 2 in the following snippet):
```
    def get_sheet_data(
        self, sheet, file_rows_needed: int | None = None
    ) -> list[list[Scalar]]:
        if self.book.read_only:
            sheet.reset_dimensions()
```
The `reset_dimensions` call resets the values.

Why is this call done, is it necessary? On read-only sheets only?! Can those two lines be removed? Unfortunately there is no comment as to why they are needed. Removing them fixes the issue for me - but would that break otherwise? In any case, I do not expect a "read" operation to change max_row and max_column.

The problem is that I need to read multiple tables from different sheets. So I usually first try to find the position of the tables in the file using openpyxl code on the excel_file.book, then I read the table using excel_file.parse with corresponding parameters (in particular skiprows and skipfooter) And afterwards I still read more stuff from the same sheet. [Excel files from customers can be a big PITA, customers like to put multiple tables one one sheet or add hidden sheets, hidden rows&cols - that would almost be a feature request: read_excel(..., read_hidden_cols=False)]

It came as a surprise that the dimensions are lost after reading.

This is an issue for openpyxl / xlsx files only: when reading an old-style xls file with xlrd instead, the sheet dimension can be found via `book.sheet_by_name("Sheet1").nrows` and `ncols` - and they do not change after reading.


### Expected Behavior

Dimensions should be left alone.

### Installed Versions

Limited to relevant parts

<details>
INSTALLED VERSIONS
------------------
python                : 3.12.3
pandas                : 2.3.3
openpyxl              : 3.1.5
</details>

The issue is that these dimensions can be unreliable, so to improve the robustness of pandas we instruct openpyxl to ignore them. I agree that having this impact the user's handle is a downside and desired to fix, but I don't think we should do so if it makes our reading less robust.

Further investigations and PRs to fix are welcome!

Ok, thanks for the info. That was not the answer I was hoping for as this means I need to modify my code and stop using `max_row` and `max_column`!
On the other hand, I guess I did not come across any broken file so far - and one could also consider this a bug elsewhere then.

I see two options:
a) just close this - and I'll modify my code to deal with this
b) if I am not mistaken, there is just one function where the change to None actually matters - and that is the `for row_number, row in enumerate(sheet.rows)` in `get_sheet_data` (line 615)  (i.e. in the iteration itself, ultimately boils down to `ReadOnlyWorksheet._cells_by_row` ). So another option would be to save the old values before calling `sheet.reset_dimensions()` and restoring them after the loop. That feels a bit "hacky" tbh.

I'd be fine with (b), but should be implemented in an error-tolerant (e.g. `try...finally...`).

query:
API: default to microseconds for Timestamp/Timedelta creation from numeric input

After the recent PRs for defaulting to microseconds when possible in `date_range`/`Timestamp`/`to_datetime` etc (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/58989), there is one main type of input to those functions that still result in nanoseconds, which is numeric input.

For example:

```
>>> pd.to_datetime([1, 2, 3], unit="s")
DatetimeIndex(['1970-01-01 00:00:01', '1970-01-01 00:00:02',
               '1970-01-01 00:00:03'],
              dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)
```

(there is the, separate, confusing part that the `unit` keyword here is define how to interpret the input, and not to specify the unit of the return value)

As a starter, I think there is no reason (apart from that it is currently implemented like that) to return nanoseconds here (unless the input are nanoseconds). 
So I would at least default to microseconds when possible. 

But then another option would also be to do as minimal conversion as possible, and for example if the input is seconds (or minutes, hours, etc) also return seconds, etc. This gives more variation in the resulting dtype, but causes less conversion.

(I have a slight preference to as much as possible return the same dtype)
hints:
cc @jbrockmendel

I'm thinking something similar, but am still tripped up by floats.  We could change the behavior for int-dtype and for object-dtype-of-ints but keep float behavior the same?  (xref #53445)

> (there is the, separate, confusing part that the unit keyword here is define how to interpret the input, and not to specify the unit of the return value)

xref #62440

> But then another option would also be to do as minmal conversion as possible, and for example if the input is seconds (or minutes, hours, etc) also return seconds, etc

I lean toward this option.

Small correction, it seems `pd.Timestamp` already takes the input unit:

```
>>> pd.Timestamp(1, unit="s").unit
's'
>>> pd.to_datetime(1, unit="s").unit
'ns'
```

(and for `date_range`, if you pass integers, it sees it as nanoseconds, the `unit` keyword there is for the return value ..)

It is for Timedelta that both are still giving nanoseconds:

```
>>> pd.Timedelta(1, unit="s").unit
'ns'
>>> pd.to_timedelta(1, unit="s").unit
'ns'
```

> I'm thinking something similar, but am still tripped up by floats. We could change the behavior for int-dtype and for object-dtype-of-ints but keep float behavior the same? (xref [#53445](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/53445))

Yes, indeed we probably have to keep floats default to nanoseconds, or we wouldn't have a consistent dtype, but very value-dependent behaviour .. For a case like this, we would need an "output" unit indication if we would ever want to change the default from nanos to microseconds

That's exactly the problem I ran into in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63272 - maybe you could close my report then to have only one open issue left? It boils down to the same problem as described here.

This should not fail:
```
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(
    pd.DataFrame({"d": pd.to_datetime(["2020-01-01"])}) + pd.Timedelta(1, unit="D"),
    pd.DataFrame({"d": pd.to_datetime(["2020-01-02"])})
)
```
Maybe all timestamps should always default to `us` unless you specify `precision="ns"` explicitly? Then there would not be any surprises and - most important - no data dependent dtypes. Otherwise it would be great to see some documentation how to not get `ns` precision in this case.

> That's exactly the problem I ran into in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63272

Indeed, that seems to be the case!


> Maybe all timestamps should always default to `us` unless you specify `precision="ns"` explicitly? Then there would not be any surprises and - most important - no data dependent dtypes.

That would be my personal preference as well, but I think we are going with preserving the input unit for this case of passing an integer to Timedelta(..) constructor with a specified `unit` (`Timestamp()` already has that behaviour, and it will also be easier to migrate to use `unit` to mean the result unit). 

But, at least in the specific example you show above, this change will prevent nanoseconds to come up. Because the result of `to_datetime` is microseconds, and then when adding a timedelta with a lower resolution like seconds, the result will keep the microseconds.

Updating this issue, I think with the three linked PRs from @jbrockmendel (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/63302, https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/63303, https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/63347), that should ensure that `Timestamp/to_datetime/Timedelta/to_timedelta` now all consistently use the input unit as result unit for _integer_ input.

The other part here was what to do about float input? We cannot just use the specified input unit because of the fractional part. When discussed at the dev meeting in December, the proposal was to still support "round" floats similarly as integers. For actual floats we can keep nanoseconds for now and decide later (deprecate or have users specify output unit). 
This was done in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/63533 and https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/63595

With that, I think this issue should be complete?

> With that, I think this issue should be complete?

I think so, yes.

Reopening this issue, triggered by https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/65608

That issue reported a side-effect of changing the default resolution (it is behaviour that already existed before, but now becomes more prevalent because of the default-unit change):

```python
>>> td = pd.Timedelta( 1, 's' )
>>> td
Timedelta('0 days 00:00:01')
>>> td.unit
'ns'     # with pandas 2.3, default is always nanoseconds
's'      # with pandas 3.0, now uses input unit (to the extent possible)
>>> td / 2
Timedelta('0 days 00:00:00.500000')  # with pandas 2.3
Timedelta('0 days 00:00:00')         # with pandas 3.0
```

Division with Timedelta always has preserved the unit, and therefore essentially does a floor division (i.e. not a division that keeps the fractional part of the result, if there is any). And so also before, a Timedelta of `1s` with "s" unit would have given this result of `0s`. But now it is much more common to get this second resolution, making the probability of running into this behaviour higher.

For most ways of constructing timedeltas, we still default to "us" resolution, and in those cases this behaviour will be in most cases less problematic. But specifically for the constructors with numeric input (i.e. this issue), we decided to not default to microseconds, but to preserve the input unit (to the extent possible).

In hindsight, at least for Timedelta(), I think there are some good arguments to default to microseconds generally (i.e. also for numeric input), even besides the division case:

- We could potentially have int vs float input behave the same (if we are OK with interpreting the fractional part of floats up to the microsecond, by default, instead of up to the nanoseconds).
- That would also make `pd.Timedelta(days=1)` vs `pd.Timedelta(1, "D")` behave the same (this looks very similar, and the user does not necessarily know that the first goes through stdlib timedelta and thus gives microseconds).
- Consistent output unit regardless of `origin` being passed or not

We discussed this again at the dev meeting (from two weeks ago), and there was some general (but not unanimous) agreement on changing the default to microseconds. However, if doing that preference was to not make such a breaking change in 3.0.4 (although it was only changed in 3.0.0), but still in 3.1.0.

BUG:  `cummax` / `cummin` incorrect for pyarrow floating dtypes

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([-4.0, -3.0, -2.0, -1.0], dtype="float64[pyarrow]")
print(s.cummax())
```

### Issue Description

`Series.cummax()` / `DataFrame.cummax()` on a pyarrow floating dtype ( `float32[pyarrow]` / `float64[pyarrow]` ) silently returns a tiny sentinel (~2.2e-308, which prints as 0.0) instead of the true running maximum whenever the running max is negative (or zero/subnormal), because the underlying `pyarrow.compute.cumulative_max` call omits start, so pyarrow defaults it to the smallest positive float instead of `-inf`. The same root cause makes `cummin` return a wrong value when the running min is `+inf` 

### Expected Behavior

`cummax` should return the true running maximum (e.g. [-4, -3, -2, -1] for [-4, -3, -2, -1]), matching the numpy-backed dtype, instead of 0.0.

BUG: Collision between equivalent frequencies 'QS-FEB' and 'QS-NOV'

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> i = pd.date_range('2020-02-01', freq='QS-MAY', periods=3)
>>> i
DatetimeIndex(['2020-02-01', '2020-05-01', '2020-08-01'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='QS-MAY')
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex(i, freq='QS-FEB')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "C:\Program Files\Python312\Lib\site-packages\pandas\core\indexes\datetimes.py", line 370, in __new__
    dtarr = DatetimeArray._from_sequence_not_strict(
            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "C:\Program Files\Python312\Lib\site-packages\pandas\core\arrays\datetimes.py", line 394, in _from_sequence_not_strict
    result._maybe_pin_freq(freq, validate_kwds)
  File "C:\Program Files\Python312\Lib\site-packages\pandas\core\arrays\datetimelike.py", line 2094, in _maybe_pin_freq
    _validate_inferred_freq(freq, self._freq)
  File "C:\Program Files\Python312\Lib\site-packages\pandas\core\arrays\datetimelike.py", line 2526, in _validate_inferred_freq
    raise ValueError(
ValueError: Inferred frequency <QuarterBegin: startingMonth=5> from passed values does not conform to passed frequency QS-FEB
```

### Issue Description

`pd.DatetimeIndex(...)`, when passed both an index with a frequency, AND a frequency, throws an error if the frequencies are unequal - even if they are equivalent.

### Expected Behavior

If the frequencies are unequal, but equivalent (like in the example), an index with the specified (new) frequency should be returned.

That the frequencies are equivalent can be seen in the following snippet: simply direct setting the frequency of `i` to the specified frequency DOES work:

```
>>> i = pd.date_range('2020-02-01', freq='QS-MAY', periods=3)
>>> i.freq = 'QS-FEB'
>>> i
DatetimeIndex(['2020-02-01', '2020-05-01', '2020-08-01'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='QS-FEB')
``` 

I think this only occurs for quarter-frequency, where "equivalent" means that the starting month mod 3 is equal.

Current workaround: 

We don't want to change `i`, so the current workaround to `i2 = pd.DatetimeIndex(i, freq='QS-FEB')` is

```
i2 = i.copy()
i2.freq = 'QS-FEB'
```
...which is cumbersome, because it requires 2 steps and cannot be used in list comprehensions etc.

Alternatively, there is the elegant

```
i2 = pd.DatetimeIndex(i, freq=None).to_frame().asfreq(i.freq).index
```

To react to your point 2.: 

One advantage of the distinction is e.g. business years starting in e.g. November. Aggregating to years, we need to use "YS-NOV". Aggregating to quarters can currently be done with "QS-NOV", which is more intuitive than having to use "QS-FEB".

However, I agree with you and think the disadvantages outweigh this advantage. And the current implementation is unreliable anyway:


**From where I'm standing, the best compromise is to have 3 main QS-frequencies (QS-JAN, -FEB, -MAR), and consider the others as aliases.**

```python

array([-9223372036854775808,  1451692800000000000,  1451779200000000000])
```

The dense version goes through `DatetimeArray.astype`, for which .astype to int64 is basically a view (xref #45034).  The Sparse version goes through `astype_nansafe` which specifically checks for NaTs when going from dt64->int64.  I expected this to match the non-sparse behavior.

When converting to `Sparse[int64]`, we only call astype_nansafe on the non-NaT elements so it doesn't raise, but when converting the fill_value from NaT it somehow gets 0, whereas I expected _that_ to raise.

Side-notes:
`ser.astype(pd.SparseDtype(ser.dtype))` raises, as does `dense.astype("Sparse[int64]")`

DEPR: `keep_default_dates` and  `convert_dates` in `read_json`

`read_json` has `convert_dates`, `keep_default_dates` and `dtypes` that all try to perform dtype conversions on the result from the ujson parser. Conflicts can arise when a column matching the specification of `keep_default_dates` matches a column specified in `dtypes`.

The proposal is to deprecate `keep_default_dates` and `convert_dates` and only use `dtype`'s current definition of

* `True`: attempt dtype conversion on all column (and refactor to use `infer_dtype` instead of `astype` guessing)
* `False`: perform no dtype conversion
* `dict`: dict keys that match column labels will be cast to type in the dict value

query:
API: read_sas should decode text by default instead of returning bytes

### Feature Type

- [X] Changing existing functionality in pandas

### Problem Description

`read_sas` defaults to `encoding=None`, which returns character columns as object-dtype `bytes`:

```python
>>> pd.read_sas("test1.sas7bdat")["Column2"]
0    b'pear'
dtype: object
```

sas7bdat files record their encoding in the header, so pandas can usually decode without being told. It is also now the only pandas reader that returns bytes by default.

### Feature Description

Deprecate the current default and change it to `encoding="infer"`, which decodes using the header-declared encoding (falling back to `latin-1` when the code is unrecognized). For XPORT, which has no encoding field, `"infer"` means `ISO-8859-1` — matching `XportReader`'s own default, which `read_sas` currently overrides with `None`.

`encoding=None` stays available for users who want raw bytes.

### Alternative Solutions

Leave the default and require every user to pass `encoding=`.

```python
# SIGSEGV, exit 139, no traceback
```

Passing self_destruct=True through to_pandas_kwargs segfaults the interpreter.

to_pandas_kwargs is 3.0 only. On 2.3.3 the argument falls through to pyarrow.parquet.read_table and raises TypeError, so this looks specific to the 3.0 passthrough.

I ran each case in its own subprocess:


| case | result |
|---|---|
| `{"self_destruct": True}` | Crashes (signal 11) |
| `{"self_destruct": True, "split_blocks": True}` | Crashes (signal 11) |
| `{"split_blocks": True}` | ok |
| `{}` | ok |
| no `to_pandas_kwargs` | ok |

BUG: tz_localize misreports wall times whose UTC value is unrepresentable (NaT sentinel, int64 wrap, OOB read)

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from dateutil.tz import gettz

# (1) Asia/Tokyo ran on LMT +09:18:59 in 1677, so this wall time's UTC value is
#     exactly iNaT.  It is unrepresentable, but nothing says so.
ts = pd.Timestamp("1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224192")

ts.tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo")
# ValueError: 1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224192 is a nonexistent time due to
# daylight savings time. Try using the 'nonexistent' argument.
#   ^ there is no DST gap here; the wall time exists, its UTC value does not

ts.tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo", nonexistent="NaT")
# NaT                                                    <- silently

ts.tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo", nonexistent="shift_forward")
# Timestamp('1677-09-21 10:00:00+091859', tz='Asia/Tokyo')   <- plausible, wrong

# (2) same thing at the top end, via the zoneinfo tz-rule fastpath
pd.Timestamp.max.tz_localize("US/Pacific")
# ValueError: 2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807 is a nonexistent time due to
# daylight savings time.

# (3) the vectorised fixed-offset path does not check at all
pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp(-(2**63) + 8 * 3600 * 10**9)]).tz_localize("Etc/GMT-8")
# DatetimeIndex(['NaT'], dtype='datetime64[ns, Etc/GMT-8]', freq=None)

pd.Series(np.array(["1677-09-21T08:12:43.145224192"], dtype="M8[ns]"),
          dtype="M8[ns, Etc/GMT-8]")
# 0   NaT
# dtype: datetime64[ns, Etc/GMT-8]

# (4) out-of-bounds read: a `nonexistent=` shift landing past the last cached
#     DST transition indexes `info.deltas` at `ntrans`.  Same call, same build:
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2015-03-08 02:30"])
dti.tz_localize(gettz("America/Boise"), nonexistent=pd.Timedelta(days=11_000))
# DatetimeIndex(['257383-01-02 22:07:35.427585-07:00'], ...)
dti.tz_localize(gettz("America/Boise"), nonexistent=pd.Timedelta(days=11_000))
# DatetimeIndex(['2045-04-18 19:30:00-07:00'], ...)

# (5) the reverse direction is unchecked too, and stores the corrupt value
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(
    np.array([pd.Timestamp.min._value], dtype="M8[ns]")
).tz_localize("UTC").tz_convert("US/Pacific")

dti.tz_localize(None)   # ['2262-04-11T15:54:18.854775809']  <- 585 years off
dti.floor("D").asi8     # [9223311600000000000]              <- stored
dti.year                # [2262]
```

### Issue Description

`NPY_NAT` is `INT64_MIN`, so it is both the `NaT` sentinel and a value that ordinary
datetime arithmetic can land on. In `pandas/_libs/tslibs/tzconversion.pyx` it is *also*
`_get_utc_bounds`' internal "no candidate found" marker, so a wall time whose true UTC
value is the sentinel is indistinguishable from one that does not exist in the zone.

This is the timezone-conversion counterpart of #66510, which covered the parsing and
construction side and was fixed by #66520. The shift-to-UTC side was not, and there are a
few adjacent problems in the same block:

**(1)–(2) The sentinel is reported as a nonexistent time.** `_get_utc_bounds` writes
`NPY_NAT` into `result_a`/`result_b` to mean "no candidate". When the real UTC value *is*
`NPY_NAT`, the caller reads that as a DST gap and takes the `nonexistent=` path — so
`"raise"` gives a wrong diagnosis, `"NaT"` silently swallows it, and the shift modes
return a wrong-but-plausible timestamp. There is a second instance in the
zoneinfo/`has_tz_rule` fastpath, which does a raw `val - delta` that can also wrap int64;
sweeping all zones shows both shapes.

**(3) The vectorised `use_fixed` and `use_tzlocal` loops have no check at all.** GH-65353
added `checked_sub` to the scalar `tz_localize_to_utc_single`, but the array loops still
do a bare `v - delta`, so `DatetimeIndex.tz_localize` / `Series.dt.tz_localize` /
tz-aware-dtype construction silently produce `NaT` or a wrapped value where the scalar
path already raises `OutOfBoundsDatetime`.

**(4) `info.deltas[ntrans]` is read out of bounds** (independent of the sentinel, and
older). In the `nonexistent=` shift block, `bisect_right_i8` returns `ntrans` when the
shifted wall time is past the last cached transition; the following
`delta_idx = delta_idx - delta_idx_offset` can leave it at `ntrans`, and `deltas` has
length `ntrans`. The result is whatever was in memory — it differs between two calls in
the same process. A wrapped shift can also drive the index to `-1`.

Worth flagging for anyone fixing (4): clamping to `ntrans - 1` is **not** correct. That
bisect compares a *wall* time against `info.tdata`, which holds *UTC* instants, so for a
zone east of UTC a wall time from before the last transition still compares greater than
it, and the clamp then applies the post-transition offset — an hour out, in roughly 90 zones.
`Asia/Anadyr` at `2011-03-27 02:30` with `nonexistent="shift_backward"` is a clean
example. It needs a walk-back to the last delta whose own UTC value falls at or after its
transition.

**(5) The reverse direction.** `Localizer.utc_val_to_local_val` does an unchecked
`utc_val + delta`, so converting a boundary UTC instant to wall time wraps by 585 years.
This one is not just a bad repr: `tz_localize(None)` and `floor`/`ceil`/`round` store the
wrapped value, and `.year` / `.strftime` agree with it. The scalar path already refuses
the same value via `conversion.check_overflows`, so scalar and array disagree.

I prototyped (5). Notes below, since the fix is less obvious than it looks.

*The wrap is universal, the sentinel is not.* A wrapped local value renders as a wildly wrong
wall time, so it is wrong for every consumer and belongs in the shift. A local value landing
*exactly on* the sentinel still renders the correct wall time through
`pandas_datetime_to_datetimestruct`, and is only unusable once stored into an i8 buffer where
`iNaT` means `NaT`. Rejecting both in the shift regresses consumers that are correct today,
including a test added by GH-66520. For

```python
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp(iNaT + 3600 * 10**9, tz="UTC")]).tz_convert(
    timezone(timedelta(hours=-1))
)   # UTC value representable, local value == iNaT
```

| consumer | today | sentinel rejected in the shift |
|---|---|---|
| `tz_localize(None)` | `NaT`, silent loss | raises ✔ |
| `.year` / `.month` | `-1`, silently wrong | raises ✔ |
| `to_period("ns")` | `NaT`, silent loss | raises ✔ |
| `to_pydatetime()` | `1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224` ✔ | regressed |
| `to_period("D")`, `astype(object)`, `.resolution`, `.is_normalized` | correct ✔ | regressed |
| `read_csv` on `1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224192-01:00` | parses ✔ | regressed — breaks `test_parse_dates_c_fastpath_nat_sentinel_shifts_into_range` |

So: checked add in the shift, sentinel rejected by the consumers that *store* it. There are
exactly two — `tz_convert_from_utc` (backs `tz_localize(None)` and everything reached via
`_local_timestamps()`), and `dt64arr_to_periodarr` at `freq="ns"` only, where the period
ordinal *is* the local i8 value. `normalize_i8_timestamps` needs nothing: local midnight can
never equal `INT64_MIN`, since `INT64_MIN % ppd != 0`.

*`is_date_array_normalized` has to change in the same commit.* It is the only `Localizer`
loop that does not skip `NPY_NAT` before shifting, so guarding the shift makes
`DatetimeIndex([NaT], tz=<negative offset>).is_normalized` raise. It needs
`if utc_val == NPY_NAT: return False`; a bare `continue` flips all-NaT arrays to `True`.
That is behaviour-preserving — across 597 pytz zones (335 distinct UTC offsets) at
`s`/`ms`/`us`/`ns`, no offset makes `(iNaT + delta) % ppd == 0`. On the DST path today it is
not defined at all: `pos == -1`, so `deltas[-1]` is an out-of-bounds read, a third instance
of (4). Nothing currently tests `is_normalized` with `NaT`.

*The message needs the target tz.* Going UTC→local the only value left to render is the
in-bounds UTC instant, so `raise_out_of_bounds` reads as nonsense — `Converting 1677-09-21
00:12:43 underflows past 1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224193`, where the named value looks fine.
An optional `to_tz` argument fixes it. The sentinel case does not need one; there the
rendered value *is* the offending local wall time.

*Cost.* The checked add is ~0.8 ns/element. As a `Localizer` method, so `tz` and `_creso`
ride along in `self`, that is +4–6% on `tz_convert_from_utc` over 1M values; as a
module-level helper taking a `tzinfo` argument it is +29% on the fixed-offset path, so the
argument passing dominates rather than the check.

*Test notes.* Zones per leg: `Asia/Tokyo` and `Pacific/Kiritimati` for the DST bisect (both
`has_tz_rule=False` — `Asia/Tokyo` is the trap, it does *not* take the fastpath),
`Europe/Berlin` + `Timestamp.max` for the zoneinfo `has_tz_rule` fastpath (transition
generation stops at 2100, so `max` lands past `last_trans`), `Etc/GMT±5` for fixed offset,
and `tm.set_timezone` + `dateutil.tz.tzlocal()` for tzlocal. Tests have to materialize:
`DatetimeIndex.tz_convert` is lazy, and so is `DatetimeIndex([<int>], tz=...)`.
`Timestamp(<int>, tz=...)` is eager, and is the most direct user-visible form of (5).
`Timestamp.replace` is not reachable — construction raises first.

### Expected Behavior

A computed `datetime64` value equal to `NPY_NAT` is unrepresentable and should raise
`OutOfBoundsDatetime`, exactly like a value one unit further out already does — not "this
is a nonexistent time", not `NaT`, not a wrapped value. `NPY_NAT + 1` (`Timestamp.min`)
must keep working, and genuine ambiguous/nonexistent handling and `NaT` passthrough must
be untouched.

```python
pd.Timestamp("1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224192").tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo")
# OutOfBoundsDatetime: Converting 1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224192 underflows past
# 1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224193

# one nanosecond later shifts to Timestamp.min and is fine
pd.Timestamp("1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224193").tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo")
# Timestamp('1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224193+091859', tz='Asia/Tokyo')
```

(4) and (5) should be deterministic and in-bounds. For (5), the wrap should raise wherever
it happens, and the sentinel should raise only where the value would be stored — see the
notes above. `utc_val_to_local_val` also backs field access, `strftime` and rounding, and
those must keep working for a local time that merely renders onto the sentinel.

Reproduced on `main` at 082e77392bd (3.1.0.dev0).

#### Problem description

Documentation for [`Series.to_json`](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/generated/pandas.Series.to_json.html#pandas.Series.to_json) appears to have been copied from `DataFrame.to_json`. 

This documentation ends up misleading the user when the user wants the Series serialised to JSON in a `records` format.

Without any arguments, the method returns a JSON object that already looks like it's formatted as `records`. However, if you do pass `records=True`, `to_json` returns only an array of values in the Series.

```python
s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
s.to_json()
```

BUG: read_sas segfaults on a SAS7BDAT file with an out-of-range row_length in the header

### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

`read_sas` segfaults on a SAS7BDAT file whose header declares a large `row_length`. No corruption of the *data* is needed — four bytes of metadata are enough.

```python
import struct
import pandas as pd

# pandas' own test file; the row_length field lives in the row-size subheader
src = "pandas/tests/io/sas/data/test1.sas7bdat"
data = bytearray(open(src, "rb").read())
assert struct.unpack("<I", data[130612:130616])[0] == 816  # row_length
data[130612:130616] = struct.pack("<I", 0x7FFFFFF0)
open("crash.sas7bdat", "wb").write(bytes(data))

pd.read_sas("crash.sas7bdat")   # Segmentation fault: 11
```

```
$ python -X faulthandler repro.py
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

Current thread 0x00000001d8f81c40 (most recent call first):
  File "pandas/io/sas/sas7bdat.py", line 736 in read
  File "pandas/io/sas/sasreader.py", line 214 in read_sas
$ echo $?
139
```

Crash report frames:

```
sas.cpython-313-darwin.so  __pyx_f_6pandas_5_libs_3sas_6Parser_process_byte_array_with_data
sas.cpython-313-darwin.so  __pyx_f_6pandas_5_libs_3sas_6Parser_readline
sas.cpython-313-darwin.so  __pyx_pw_6pandas_5_libs_3sas_6Parser_9read
EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV), KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS
```

### Issue Description

`Parser.process_byte_array_with_data` takes its bounds as C `int`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/_libs/sas.pyx#L541

```cython
cdef void process_byte_array_with_data(self, int offset, int length) except *:
    ...
    assert offset + length <= self.cached_page_len, "Out of bounds read"
    source = Buffer(&self.cached_page[offset], length)
```

`length` is `row_length`, read straight from the file as an unsigned int. When it is near `INT_MAX`, `offset + length` overflows signed `int` and wraps negative, so the guard passes. `Buffer` is then constructed with a ~2GB `length` over a 64KB page. `buf_get`'s own `assert offset < buf.length` is satisfied for reads far past the real allocation, so every subsequent read is unchecked and the process dies on a wild address.

A more modest `row_length` (e.g. `0x20000000`) is caught cleanly by the assert — it is specifically the overflow that defeats it. Widening these parameters to `int64_t`/`Py_ssize_t` and validating `row_length` against the page size after parsing the row-size subheader would fix it.

This is **not** fixed by #66469, which validates
`offsets[j] + lengths[j] <= row_length` once in `Parser.__init__`. That check passes
trivially here — the column offsets and lengths are untouched, it is `row_length` itself
that is out of range — so the crash above reproduces with #66469 applied.

Two related unchecked accesses in the same loop, noted for completeness:

1. The 8-byte fast path added in #65363 reads without a bounds check, unlike the `else`
   branch it replaced, which used the checked `buf_get`. **Already fixed by #66469**;
   mentioned here only because it shares this function and I hit it while narrowing down
   the crash.

2. The function is `@cython.boundscheck(False)` / `@cython.wraparound(False)`, and the
   destination index `m = s + 8 - lngt` goes negative for a decimal column declaring
   `lngt > 8`. Nothing validates `3 <= lngt <= 8`, and #66469's check does not catch it
   either (a column can declare `lngt > 8` while still fitting inside the row). Patching
   column 0 of `test1.sas7bdat` to declare length 16 does not crash, but writes 8 bytes
   in front of `byte_chunk` and returns a silently wrong frame.

`row_count`, `column_count`, and the subheader offset/length pairs are also file-controlled
and reach this arithmetic; a too-large `column_count` is caught, but only incidentally, by
an `IndexError` in `_parse_metadata`.

### Expected Behavior

A malformed or truncated SAS7BDAT should raise, not segfault. `test_corrupt_read` already covers a truncated file, so the intent is there — it just does not extend to metadata whose values are internally inconsistent.

This matters beyond developer error: `.sas7bdat` files are routinely received from third parties, so the parser is effectively parsing untrusted input.

BUG: IntervalArray silently builds interval[int64] with an object-dtype right side

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

arr = pd.arrays.IntervalArray([pd.Interval(0, 2**64)])

arr.dtype          # interval[int64, right]
arr.dtype.subtype  # int64
arr.left.dtype     # int64
arr.right.dtype    # object     <- contradicts the advertised subtype
arr.length.dtype   # object
arr.mid.dtype      # object

# the mirror image, with the oversized value on the left, is rejected
pd.arrays.IntervalArray([pd.Interval(-(2**64), 0)])
# TypeError: category, object, and string subtypes are not supported for IntervalArray
```

`pd.IntervalIndex([pd.Interval(0, 2**64)])` produces the same inconsistent state.

### Issue Description

When only the *right* endpoint falls outside the `int64` range, `IntervalArray` builds an array
whose declared dtype disagrees with its own data: `dtype` says `interval[int64, right]` while
`right.dtype` is `object`. Every derived quantity inherits the inconsistency (`length`, `mid`),
and `arr.astype(arr.dtype)` does not repair it.

`IntervalArray._ensure_simple_new_inputs` only ever consults `left.dtype`:

- the object/category/string rejection checks `left.dtype` alone
  ([interval.py:324](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/arrays/interval.py#L324)), so an object
  *right* side passes;
- the dtype is then derived from `left.dtype` alone
  ([interval.py:365](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/arrays/interval.py#L365));
- the signed/unsigned mismatch check
  ([interval.py:370-378](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/arrays/interval.py#L370-L378))
  requires *both* `left_dtype.kind` and `right_dtype.kind` to be in `"iu"`, so an `object` right
  side (kind `"O"`) skips that guard too.

The asymmetry is the clearest symptom: putting the oversized value on the left raises a clean
`TypeError`, while putting it on the right silently produces a corrupt array.

### Expected Behavior

Either outcome would be consistent; the current side-dependent behavior is not:

- raise the same `TypeError` regardless of which endpoint has the unsupported dtype, or
- derive the subtype from both endpoints so the resulting `dtype` actually describes the data.

At minimum `arr.dtype.subtype` should never disagree with `arr.left.dtype` / `arr.right.dtype`.

### Installed Versions

<details>

```
INSTALLED VERSIONS
------------------
commit                : e68db09ecf6427d1b62e565bacf17f2e525a3032
python                : 3.13.11
python-bits           : 64
OS                    : Darwin
OS-release            : 23.3.0
pandas                : 3.0.5
numpy                 : 2.5.1
dateutil              : 2.9.0.post0
```

Also reproduced on main at 7986b42596f.

</details>

BUG: DataFrame.stack raises a bare AssertionError when level contains duplicate entries

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

columns = pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
    [["A", "B"], ["c", "d"], ["e", "f"]], names=["l0", "l1", "l2"]
)
df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(8).reshape(1, 8), columns=columns)

df.stack([0, 0])        # AssertionError, with no message
df.stack(["l0", "l0"])  # AssertionError, with no message
df.stack([1, -2])       # AssertionError, with no message
df.stack([2, -1])       # IndexError: pop index out of range
```

### Issue Description

Passing a `level` list that contains duplicate entries to `DataFrame.stack` fails with an
internal error instead of a user-facing one:

```
  File "pandas/core/reshape/reshape.py", line 1023, in stack_v3
    assert isinstance(stack_cols, MultiIndex)
AssertionError
```

`stack_v3` computes the columns to stack from the deduplicated `set(level)`:

```python
set_levels = set(level)
stack_cols = frame.columns._drop_level_numbers(
    [k for k in range(frame.columns.nlevels - 1, -1, -1) if k not in set_levels]
)
```

but later branches on the length of the original, non-deduplicated list:

```python
if len(level) > 1:
    sorter = np.argsort(level)
    assert isinstance(stack_cols, MultiIndex)
```

With `level=[0, 0]`, `set_levels` has one entry, so `stack_cols` is a plain `Index`, while
`len(level)` is still 2 and the assertion fires.

Note that the duplicates need not be written literally. `DataFrame.stack` resolves level
names and negative level numbers with `_get_level_number` before reaching `stack_v3`, so on
3-level columns `["l0", "l0"]`, `[1, -2]` and `[2, -1]` all normalize to duplicated level
numbers and hit the same code path.

This is also a change in behavior from the previous implementation, which accepted duplicate
levels and stacked sequentially:

```python
>>> df.stack([0, 0], future_stack=False)  # legacy implementation
l2       e  f
  l0 l1
0 A  c   1  2
     d   3  4
  B  c   5  6
     d   7  8

>>> df.stack(0).stack(0)  # identical result
```

### Expected Behavior

An informative exception rather than a bare `AssertionError` or an `IndexError` from an
internal `list.pop`.

There are two defensible behaviors, so I wanted to raise it rather than pick one silently:

1. **Raise an informative `ValueError`.** The current implementation stacks the specified
   original column levels simultaneously, and "the same level twice" has no meaning in that
   model. `stack_v3` already raises `ValueError("Columns with duplicate values are not
   supported in stack")` for the analogous duplicate-column case. This also avoids silently
   choosing semantics that differ from the legacy implementation, which stacked two distinct
   levels for `[0, 0]`.
2. **Deduplicate**, so that `stack([0, 0])` behaves as `stack([0])`. This would match the
   sibling APIs, which all accept duplicate levels today: `unstack([0, 0])`,
   `groupby(level=[0, 0])`, `droplevel([0, 0])` and `reorder_levels` all succeed. The
   downside is that it silently changes the legacy result rather than flagging it.

I have a PR ready implementing option 1, following the precedent of #25413, where `concat`
with `keys` was changed to raise an informative `ValueError` instead of an `AssertionError`.
Happy to switch it to option 2 if maintainers prefer consistency with `unstack`.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Built from source at current `main` (1b1e271f30b3ac77a051dc8293294d7b526db87e), Python 3.13.1,
NumPy 2.5.1, Windows 11 (x86_64, MSVC build).

</details>

+            f"level should not contain duplicate values, got level numbers {level}"
+        )

         return frame
     set_levels = set(level)

BUG: segfault on next() after a chunked read_csv chunk raised (C engine)

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import io

import pandas as pd

# column "b" has one non-numeric token, so converting the first chunk raises
data = "a,b\n" + "".join(f"{i},{'oops' if i == 5 else i}\n" for i in range(20))

reader = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), dtype={"b": "int64"}, chunksize=10)

try:
    next(reader)
except ValueError:
    pass  # invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'oops'

next(reader)  # <-- segfault
```

### Issue Description

If converting a chunk raises, the `TextFileReader` is left in a state where the
next `next()` / `get_chunk()` call segfaults instead of raising.

The exception from the first chunk is the expected one:

```
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'oops'
```

The second call crashes the interpreter. `faulthandler` puts it inside the
Cython `TextReader.read` call:

```
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

Current thread 0x00000001d8f81c40 (most recent call first):
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/c_parser_wrapper.py", line 234 in read
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1923 in read
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1985 in get_chunk
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1843 in __next__
```

Scope, from varying the reproducer (identical results on 3.0.5 and 2.3.3):

| variant | result |
| --- | --- |
| `engine="c"`, `chunksize=10` | **segfault** |
| `engine="c"`, `iterator=True` + `get_chunk(10)` | **segfault** |
| `engine="c"`, `converters=` raising on row 5 instead of `dtype=` | **segfault** |
| `engine="python"`, `chunksize=10` | raises `ValueError`, no crash |
| `engine="c"`, no `dtype=` (first chunk does not raise) | fine |

So it is specific to the C parser, and what sets it up is that a chunk raised
during conversion — `dtype=` is just a convenient way to trigger that, and a
raising `converters=` callable does it too.

Not a regression: reproduces identically on 3.0.5, on 2.3.3, and on a source
build of current `main`. Nothing string- or pyarrow-specific is involved — the
reproducer has no string column.

### Expected Behavior

The second `next(reader)` should either raise a Python-level exception or return
the remaining rows. Crashing the interpreter is never acceptable, and it is
particularly bad here because catching a per-chunk conversion error and
continuing is a natural pattern for a chunked read.

Root-caused this. When _convert_column_data raises mid-conversion (the bad int token), it raises before self.parser_start += end - start, and parser_consume_rows in _read_rows also never runs — so the tokenizer has advanced its stream position and buffered the rows, but parser_start is still 0 and the buffer is never consumed. The next read sees buffered_lines >= nrows, skips re-tokenizing, and re-converts the stale buffer, which segfaults.

Two ways to fix: (A) mark the reader as errored on a failed conversion so the next read/get_chunk raises a clean ValueError instead of re-reading, or (B) advance past the failed chunk on the error path so the next read returns the remaining rows. Given the Non-Recoverable Error label I'm inclined toward (A) — happy to send a PR. Which behavior do you want?

BUG: datetimelike arithmetic landing on the NaT sentinel returns NaT, plus float64 precision loss in timedelta64 arithmetic/reductions

Follow-up to GH-66510 / GH-66520, which fixed the *parsing and construction* half of the "value lands on the `NaT` sentinel" problem (`parsers.pyx`, `conversion.pyx`, `strptime.pyx`, `Timestamp.replace`). The *arithmetic* half is still open, and while investigating it I found an adjacent family of `float64` precision bugs in `timedelta64` arithmetic and reductions.

All reproducers below are against `082e77392bd` (main as of 2026-07-29).

Two distinct root causes, filed together because they were found together and overlap in the code they touch — happy to split into separate issues if that's easier to triage.

---

## 1. `NPY_NAT` is `int64.min`, so arithmetic landing on it silently becomes `NaT`

A computed value equal to `NPY_NAT` is perfectly representable in `int64`, but is indistinguishable from `NaT` once stored. Today it is silently read back as `NaT` rather than raising. This affects scalars and arrays across all four datetimelike types.

The scalar and vectorized paths also disagree about *which* error to raise one step further out, so you can't paper over it with a `try/except`.

```python
import pandas as pd
from pandas import Timedelta, Timestamp
from pandas.core.dtypes.dtypes import PeriodDtype

# one ns past the bound -> NaT; two ns past -> raises
Timedelta.min - Timedelta(1, "ns")                  # NaT          <- should raise
Timedelta.min - Timedelta(2, "ns")                  # OverflowError

pd.array([Timedelta.min]) - Timedelta(1, "ns")      # <TimedeltaArray> [NaT]   <- should raise

Timestamp.min.as_unit("ns") - Timedelta(1, "ns")    # NaT          <- should raise
pd.to_datetime([Timestamp.min]).as_unit("ns") - Timedelta(1, "ns")
                                                    # DatetimeIndex(['NaT'])   <- should raise

per = pd.Period._from_ordinal(-(2**63) + 1, PeriodDtype("ns"))
per - 1                                             # NaT          <- should raise
pd.PeriodIndex([per]) - 1                           # PeriodIndex(['NaT'])     <- should raise
```

Notes on the vectorized side: `mul_overflowsafe` got an explicit sentinel check in GH-43178 / GH-65515, but `add_overflowsafe` never did — which is why the `timedelta64`, `datetime64` and Period-ordinal array paths above all still return `NaT`.

### 1b. The same condition surfaces as a message-less `AssertionError`

`_timedelta_from_value_and_reso` guards with a bare `assert value != NPY_NAT`, so a user hitting this gets an `AssertionError` with no message (and nothing at all under `python -O`):

```python
Timestamp.min - Timestamp(1)      # AssertionError:
Timedelta(2, "ns") * (-(2**62))   # AssertionError:
```

---

## 2. `float64` precision loss in `timedelta64` arithmetic and reductions

Separate root cause: several paths round-trip `int64` values through `float64`, which only has a 53-bit mantissa. This produces wrong answers well away from the bounds, not just at them.

### 2a. Scalar `Timedelta.__mul__` / `__truediv__`

Integral operands are applied in `float64`, so an exactly-representable result comes back wrong, or wrongly raises:

```python
Timedelta.min / 1      # AssertionError    <- should be Timedelta.min
Timedelta.max / 1      # OverflowError     <- should be Timedelta.max
Timedelta.min * 1.0    # AssertionError    <- should be Timedelta.min

# off-by-one above 2**53; numpy and Series/2 both give ...983
Timedelta(36028797018963967, "ns") / 2                          # 18014398509481984 ns
np.timedelta64(36028797018963967, "ns") / 2                     # 18014398509481983 ns
```

`__mul__` also never normalizes numpy integer scalars, so the product stays an `int64` multiply and **wraps silently** — while the Python-`int` and vectorized forms both raise:

```python
Timedelta(2**62, "ns") * np.int64(4)   # Timedelta('0 days')   <- silent wrap (RuntimeWarning only)
Timedelta(2**62, "ns") * 4             # OverflowError
pd.Series([Timedelta(2**62, "ns")]) * np.int64(4)
                                       # OutOfBoundsTimedelta: Overflow in int64 multiplication
```

`__truediv__` already does `if isinstance(other, cnp.integer): other = int(other)`; `__mul__` does not.

### 2b. `Series.sum` / `DataFrame.sum` accumulate in `float64`

`nansum` sets `dtype_sum = np.float64` for `kind == "m"`, so every `timedelta64` sum loses precision above `2**53`. A *single representable value* does not survive a round trip:

```python
Series([Timedelta.min]).sum()
# NaT                       <- should be Timedelta.min

Series([Timedelta(2**62 + 1, "ns"), Timedelta(-(2**62), "ns")]).sum()
# Timedelta('0 days')       <- should be 1 ns

Series([Timedelta(2**53 + 1, "ns"), Timedelta(0, "ns")]).sum()._value
# 9007199254740992          <- should be 9007199254740993
```

The existing `np.fabs(result) > lib.i8max` guard in `_wrap_results` cannot catch a sum of exactly `int64.min`, because `fabs(-2**63)` and `float(i8max)` are the *same* `float64`.

### 2c. `Series.cumsum` / `DataFrame.cumsum` have no overflow check at all

`_cum_func` runs `np.cumsum` straight on the `i8` view, so a running total past the bounds **wraps silently** to an unrelated value:

```python
Series([Timedelta.max] * 2).cumsum()
# [Timedelta('106751 days 23:47:16.854775807'), Timedelta('-1 days +23:59:59.999999998')]

Series([Timedelta(2**62, "ns")] * 3).cumsum()
# [Timedelta('53375 days ...'), NaT, Timedelta('-53376 days ...')]
```

---

## Expected behaviour

For (1): reject the sentinel rather than returning `NaT`, in both the scalar and vectorized paths, and replace the bare `assert` with a real exception carrying a message.

Worth deciding explicitly: the scalar `Timedelta` add/sub path should probably raise `OverflowError` rather than `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`, since `OutOfBoundsTimedelta` is a `ValueError` subclass and so would *not* actually make the scalar and array paths agree — which is the point of the change.

For (2): compute exactly in `int64` and raise on genuine overflow, instead of round-tripping through `float64`.

## Not covered above

`groupby(...).sum()` has the same sentinel hole, via a separate accumulator in `libgroupby`'s `group_sum` rather than `nanops`:

```python
half = Timedelta(-(2**62), "ns")
Series([half, half]).groupby([0, 0]).sum()   # [NaT]
```

The issue appears to be in this section of the code:  https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/e51039afe3cbdedbf5ffd5cefb5dea98c2050b88/pandas/_libs/tslibs/conversion.pyx#L214-L232

```
>>> np.int32(0) - 0

```
but with NumPy >= 2, `frac` is of type `np.int32`:
```
>>> np.int32(0) - 0
np.int32(0)
```
Further, NumPy >= 2 then raises when the `np.int32` `frac` is multiplied by `m`, which is a Python integer:
```
>>> np.int32(0) * 86400000000000
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
OverflowError: Python integer 86400000000000 out of bounds for int32
```
I believe this change in behavior is described more fully in [NEP 50](https://numpy.org/neps/nep-0050-scalar-promotion.html#nep-50-promotion-rules-for-python-scalars).  What do we think the cleanest way to address this might be?  It seems some sort of manual type promotion will be necessary (or perhaps just not using `frac` if `ts` is an integer, since it should always be zero).

BUG: Series.dt.to_pydatetime() returns a Series with a reset RangeIndex instead of preserving the parent index

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-02-01", "2026-03-01"]), index=[10, 11, 12])

print(s.dt.to_pydatetime().index)  # RangeIndex(start=0, stop=3, step=1)
print(s.dt.date.index)             # Index([10, 11, 12], dtype='int64')
print(s.dt.normalize().index)      # Index([10, 11, 12], dtype='int64')

 practical consequence is silent misalignment whenever the result is combined
with anything carrying the original index — for example a `groupby` slice, whose
index does not start at zero for any group after the first:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "g": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
    "ts": pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-04"]),
    "x": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
})

for key, sub in df.groupby("g"):
    out = pd.DataFrame({"ts": sub["ts"].dt.to_pydatetime(), "x": sub["x"]})
    print(key, len(sub), "->", len(out))


Output:


a 2 -> 2
b 2 -> 4


Group `b` is silently doubled and half-NaN:


                    ts    x
0  2026-01-03 00:00:00  NaN
1  2026-01-04 00:00:00  NaN
2                  NaN  3.0
3                  NaN  4.0
```

### Issue Description

`Series.dt.to_pydatetime()` changed from returning an `ndarray` (pandas 2.x) to
returning a `Series` (pandas 3.0). That return-type change was deprecated ahead
of time and is not what this report is about.

The problem is that the new `Series` is built without the parent index:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/indexes/accessors.py

```python
def to_pydatetime(self) -> Series:
    # GH#20306
    from pandas import Series

    return Series(self._get_values().to_pydatetime(), dtype=object)
```

There is no `index=self._parent.index`, so the result always comes back on a
fresh `RangeIndex`. Every other `.dt` accessor result preserves the index, which
makes this an inconsistency rather than a deliberate choice as far as I can tell.

It fails silently: no exception and no warning. Code that used to get an
index-free `ndarray` under 2.x, and therefore aligned positionally, now aligns on
a `RangeIndex` that happens to be wrong. Where the original index is contiguous
from 0 the results still agree, so the breakage is invisible in the common case
and appears only on reindexed or grouped data.

Two smaller points in the same area:

1. The docstring's `Returns` section still reads `numpy.ndarray` /
   "Object dtype array containing native Python datetime objects", which no
   longer matches the annotated `-> Series` return type.
2. `ArrowTemporalProperties.to_pydatetime()` takes a different path
   (`ArrowExtensionArray._dt_to_pydatetime()`), so it is worth confirming the two
   accessors agree on index handling once this is fixed.

### Expected Behavior

`s.dt.to_pydatetime()` should return a `Series` carrying `s`'s index, consistent
with `s.dt.date`, `s.dt.normalize()`, and the other `.dt` accessors:

```
Series(self._get_values().to_pydatetime(), index=self._parent.index, dtype=object)
```

DOC: Documentation unclear on how to use read_xml() with xpath parameter and a default namespace

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_xml.html



### Documentation problem

In read_xml(), there is the following note under the `namespaces` parameter:

> Note: if XML document uses default namespace denoted as xmlns=’<URI>’ without a prefix, you must assign any temporary namespace prefix such as ‘doc’ to the URI in order to parse underlying nodes and/or attributes. 

However, the way this is used is unintuitive, and I struggled to make it work.  I think better examples would be very helpful.

The current examples show the following sequence:
1. xml document with a default namespace, call to read_xml() without an `xpath` parameter
2. slightly different xml document without a namespace, call to read_xml() with `xpath` parameter
3. same xml document, now with a namespace prefix. Call to read_xml() with `xpath` and `namespaces` parameter.

A key point that is missing, in my opinion, is that read_xml() will fail with the document from the first example if we use the `xpath` parameter. The note for the `namespaces` parameter mentioned above points towards the solution, but doesn't fully explain it. In addition to assigning a temporary namespace prefix, we need to update our xpath query to use the temporary prefix. The following example illustrates this:

```
from io import StringIO
xml = '''<?xml version='1.0' encoding='utf-8'?>
<data xmlns="http://example.com">
 <row>
   <shape>square</shape>
   <degrees>360</degrees>
   <sides>4.0</sides>
 </row>
 <row>
   <shape>circle</shape>
   <degrees>360</degrees>
   <sides/>
 </row>
 <row>
   <shape>triangle</shape>
   <degrees>180</degrees>
   <sides>3.0</sides>
 </row>
</data>'''
```

```
# Using xpath in a xml with default namespace

# Attempt 1 - No namespaces parameter
try:
    df = pd.read_xml(StringIO(xml), xpath=".//row")
except ValueError as e:  # Crashes because lxml xpath does not understand default namespace
    print(e)
```

```
>>> xpath does not return any nodes or attributes. Be sure to specify in `xpath` the parent nodes of children and attributes to parse. If document uses namespaces denoted with xmlns, be sure to define namespaces and use them in xpath.
```

```
# Attempt 2 - Namespaces parameter 
try: 
    df = pd.read_xml(StringIO(xml), xpath=".//row", 
                     namespaces={"doc": "http://example.com"})
except ValueError as e:  # Crashes because our patch maps the default namespace to arbitrary prefix `doc`
    print(e)
```

```
>>> xpath does not return any nodes or attributes. Be sure to specify in `xpath` the parent nodes of children and attributes to parse. If document uses namespaces denoted with xmlns, be sure to define namespaces and use them in xpath.
```

```
# Attempt 3 - Namespaces parameter, updated xpath query
df = pd.read_xml(StringIO(xml), xpath="//doc:row", 
                 namespaces={"doc": "http://example.com"})  # Note: Make sure this matches the default namespace URI
df
```

```
      shape  degrees  sides
0    square      360    4.0
1    circle      360    NaN
2  triangle      180    3.0
```

### Suggested fix for documentation

I would add the following example to read_xml() after the 6th example block, to clarify the scenario discussed above.

```
xml = '''<?xml version='1.0' encoding='utf-8'?>
<data xmlns="http://example.com">
 <row>
   <shape>square</shape>
   <degrees>360</degrees>
   <sides>4.0</sides>
 </row>
 <row>
   <shape>circle</shape>
   <degrees>360</degrees>
   <sides/>
 </row>
 <row>
   <shape>triangle</shape>
   <degrees>180</degrees>
   <sides>3.0</sides>
 </row>
</data>'''
```

```
# If we want to use xpath with a xml document that has a default namespace, we need to:
# - assign a temporary prefix to the default namespace URI, pass it in the namespaces param
# - Update the XPath to use this temporary prefix

df = pd.read_xml(StringIO(xml), 
                 xpath="//doc:row", 
                 namespaces={"doc": "http://example.com"})   
```

### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# Sample DataFrame
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Department": ["HR", "HR", "Finance", "Finance", "IT", "IT", "Finance", "HR", "IT", "Finance"],
    "Gender": ["F", "M", "M", "F", "M", "F", "M", "F", "M", "F"],
    "Location": ["NY", "CA", "CA", "NY", "CA", "NY", "CA", "CA", "CA", "NY"]
})

    df
    .value_counts(subset=["Department", "Gender", "Location"])
    .unstack(fill_value=0, sort=False)
)

Department Gender        
Finance    F        0   2
           M        2   0
HR         F        1   1
           M        1   0
IT         F        0   1
           M        2   0
```

### Issue Description

In Pandas (v2.3), I have noticed an issue with `.unstack(fill_value=0, sort=False)` where incorrect column labels are assigned to column values.

For example, if you add the `sort=False`, the counts are not correct:
```python
print(
    df
    .value_counts(subset=["Department", "Gender", "Location"])
    .unstack(fill_value=0, sort=False)
)
```

```
Department Gender        
Finance    F        0   2
           M        2   0
IT         M        2   1
HR         F        1   0
           M        0   1
IT         F        1   0
```

Note that the dataframe contains no female in the Finnance department in CA.

I have seen related bug reports (#55516 and #53910) where this argument is supposed to be deprecated. But it seems that no warning is being issued for the deprecation.

### Expected Behavior

The following works as expected:
```python
# note: use the above "reproducible" code to generate the `df`
print(
    df
    .value_counts(subset=["Department", "Gender", "Location"])
    .unstack(fill_value=0) # without sort argument
)
```

### Issue Description

When assigning pd.NA (or other None-types) to a string-column in a dataframe with two or more string-columns, it eventually fails with an "Unknown error: Wrapping ... failed" when the dataframes are large enough. If you decrease the size of either dataframe in the reproducible example the error goes away. I've confirmed that it happens both on pandas main-branch (3.1.0.dev0+218.gea4d2c0b27) and 3.0.1.

Only happens with Pandas and PyArrow. It doesn't always happen on the first pd.NA assignment (thus the for loop). Also, it only happens with two or more string columns in the dataframe, if column "b" is dropped, the issue goes away. If you set elements with single indices `df.loc[0, "a"] = pd.NA` instead, the error also seems to dissapear.

From my investigations, it only seems to happen when the total size in memory of the column in the dataframe after the concat is above a certain threshold. Meaning that if you increase the length of the strings in column "a", the threshold in order to trigger the error decreases. Example of a shorter dataframe that also fails:
```python
df = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({"a": ["xx"] * 18, "b": ["x"] * 18}),
    pd.DataFrame({"a": ["xx"] * 17, "b": ["x"] * 17}),
])
```
The size of the strings in column "b" doesn't seem to impact if an error occurs or not.

If you set more elements to pd.NA at the same time, the threshold for when the error occurs increases. Example:
```python
df = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({"a": ["x"] * 36, "b": ["x"] * 36}),
    pd.DataFrame({"a": ["x"] * 35, "b": ["x"] * 35}),
])

for i in range(1, 50):
    df.loc[[0, 1, 2], "a"] = pd.NA
```
Here the size of the dataframe had to be increased to trigger the error.

A workaround is to set the storage type of the dataframes to "python":
```python
df = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({"a": ["x"] * 33, "b": ["x"] * 33}, dtype=pd.StringDtype(storage="python")),
    pd.DataFrame({"a": ["x"] * 34, "b": ["x"] * 34}, dtype=pd.StringDtype(storage="python")),
])
```

I've never raised an issue on github before so I'd be grateful for some feedback on anything that could be improved :)

### Expected Behavior

The expected behavior is that no errors happen, and the first row in column "a" is pd.NA.

BUG: to_json(date_format="epoch") ignores date_unit for datetime-likes behind Categorical/Sparse dtypes

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

ser = pd.Series(pd.to_datetime(["2020-01-01", "2020-01-02"]).as_unit("ns"))

# plain datetime64 column: correct
ser.to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit="s")
# '{"0":1577836800,"1":1577923200}'

# behind a Categorical: date_unit is ignored, values written in the categories' own unit
ser.astype("category").to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit="s")
# '{"0":1577836800000000000,"1":1577923200000000000}'

# same for index labels
pd.Series([1, 2], index=pd.CategoricalIndex(ser)).to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit="s")
# '{"1577836800000000000":1,"1577923200000000000":2}'

# behind a Sparse dtype: raises
ser.astype(pd.SparseDtype("M8[ns]")).to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit="s")
# AttributeError: Can only use .dt accessor with datetimelike values
```


### Issue Description

For `date_format="epoch"`, datetime-like values held behind a dtype that is not itself
`datetime64`/`timedelta64` are not scaled to `date_unit`:

- `Categorical[datetime64]` / `Categorical[timedelta64]` column values, and `CategoricalIndex`
  index or column labels, are written as epoch integers in the *categories'* resolution,
  silently ignoring `date_unit`. The value is off by a factor of 1000-1000000000 rather than
  merely imprecise, so it decodes as a completely different timestamp.
- `Sparse[datetime64]` / `Sparse[timedelta64]` raises `AttributeError` instead of serializing.

`to_json()` converts datetime-likes to `date_unit` up front, gated on `dtype.kind in ["M", "m"]`
and applied with `.dt.as_unit(date_unit)`. `CategoricalDtype.kind` is `"O"`, so categorical
datetimes never enter that branch, and nothing scales them afterwards -- the C encoder's
epoch path assumes the values it receives have already been scaled. `SparseDtype.kind`
reports the *subtype's* kind, so sparse datetimes do enter the branch, and then fail because
there is no `.dt` accessor for them.

The scaling used to happen inside the C encoder (`scaleNanosecToUnit` in
`objToJSON.c::Object_beginTypeContext`), which covered these dtypes because it worked off the
values that actually reached the encoder. GH-63100 cast to nanoseconds in
`DatetimeLikeArrayMixin._values_for_json` to make it correct for non-nano resolutions; GH-63666
then reverted that cast and moved the conversion to the Python pre-pass described above,
removing the C-side scaling. That is where the Categorical and Sparse cases fell through.

Only `date_format="epoch"` is affected -- the `"iso"` path passes the array's own unit into the
C conversion and is correct for all of these dtypes.

### Expected Behavior

Serializing with `date_format="epoch"` should produce the same output whether or not the
datetime-like values sit behind another dtype, i.e. for every `date_unit`:

```python
ser.astype("category").to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit=unit) == \
    ser.to_json(date_format="epoch", date_unit=unit)
```

and `Sparse[datetime64]` should serialize rather than raise.

### Installed Versions

<details>

pandas main (3.1.0.dev0), also reproduces on 3.0.x.

</details>
