BUG: tz_localize misreports wall times whose UTC value is unrepresentable (NaT sentinel, int64 wrap, OOB read)

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from dateutil.tz import gettz

# (1) Asia/Tokyo ran on LMT +09:18:59 in 1677, so this wall time's UTC value is
#     exactly iNaT.  It is unrepresentable, but nothing says so.
ts = pd.Timestamp("1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224192")

ts.tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo")
# ValueError: 1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224192 is a nonexistent time due to
# daylight savings time. Try using the 'nonexistent' argument.
#   ^ there is no DST gap here; the wall time exists, its UTC value does not

ts.tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo", nonexistent="NaT")
# NaT                                                    <- silently

ts.tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo", nonexistent="shift_forward")
# Timestamp('1677-09-21 10:00:00+091859', tz='Asia/Tokyo')   <- plausible, wrong

# (2) same thing at the top end, via the zoneinfo tz-rule fastpath
pd.Timestamp.max.tz_localize("US/Pacific")
# ValueError: 2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807 is a nonexistent time due to
# daylight savings time.

# (3) the vectorised fixed-offset path does not check at all
pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp(-(2**63) + 8 * 3600 * 10**9)]).tz_localize("Etc/GMT-8")
# DatetimeIndex(['NaT'], dtype='datetime64[ns, Etc/GMT-8]', freq=None)

pd.Series(np.array(["1677-09-21T08:12:43.145224192"], dtype="M8[ns]"),
          dtype="M8[ns, Etc/GMT-8]")
# 0   NaT
# dtype: datetime64[ns, Etc/GMT-8]

# (4) out-of-bounds read: a `nonexistent=` shift landing past the last cached
#     DST transition indexes `info.deltas` at `ntrans`.  Same call, same build:
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2015-03-08 02:30"])
dti.tz_localize(gettz("America/Boise"), nonexistent=pd.Timedelta(days=11_000))
# DatetimeIndex(['257383-01-02 22:07:35.427585-07:00'], ...)
dti.tz_localize(gettz("America/Boise"), nonexistent=pd.Timedelta(days=11_000))
# DatetimeIndex(['2045-04-18 19:30:00-07:00'], ...)

# (5) the reverse direction is unchecked too, and stores the corrupt value
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(
    np.array([pd.Timestamp.min._value], dtype="M8[ns]")
).tz_localize("UTC").tz_convert("US/Pacific")

dti.tz_localize(None)   # ['2262-04-11T15:54:18.854775809']  <- 585 years off
dti.floor("D").asi8     # [9223311600000000000]              <- stored
dti.year                # [2262]
```

### Issue Description

`NPY_NAT` is `INT64_MIN`, so it is both the `NaT` sentinel and a value that ordinary
datetime arithmetic can land on. In `pandas/_libs/tslibs/tzconversion.pyx` it is *also*
`_get_utc_bounds`' internal "no candidate found" marker, so a wall time whose true UTC
value is the sentinel is indistinguishable from one that does not exist in the zone.

This is the timezone-conversion counterpart of #66510, which covered the parsing and
construction side and was fixed by #66520. The shift-to-UTC side was not, and there are a
few adjacent problems in the same block:

**(1)–(2) The sentinel is reported as a nonexistent time.** `_get_utc_bounds` writes
`NPY_NAT` into `result_a`/`result_b` to mean "no candidate". When the real UTC value *is*
`NPY_NAT`, the caller reads that as a DST gap and takes the `nonexistent=` path — so
`"raise"` gives a wrong diagnosis, `"NaT"` silently swallows it, and the shift modes
return a wrong-but-plausible timestamp. There is a second instance in the
zoneinfo/`has_tz_rule` fastpath, which does a raw `val - delta` that can also wrap int64;
sweeping all zones shows both shapes.

**(3) The vectorised `use_fixed` and `use_tzlocal` loops have no check at all.** GH-65353
added `checked_sub` to the scalar `tz_localize_to_utc_single`, but the array loops still
do a bare `v - delta`, so `DatetimeIndex.tz_localize` / `Series.dt.tz_localize` /
tz-aware-dtype construction silently produce `NaT` or a wrapped value where the scalar
path already raises `OutOfBoundsDatetime`.

**(4) `info.deltas[ntrans]` is read out of bounds** (independent of the sentinel, and
older). In the `nonexistent=` shift block, `bisect_right_i8` returns `ntrans` when the
shifted wall time is past the last cached transition; the following
`delta_idx = delta_idx - delta_idx_offset` can leave it at `ntrans`, and `deltas` has
length `ntrans`. The result is whatever was in memory — it differs between two calls in
the same process. A wrapped shift can also drive the index to `-1`.

Worth flagging for anyone fixing (4): clamping to `ntrans - 1` is **not** correct. That
bisect compares a *wall* time against `info.tdata`, which holds *UTC* instants, so for a
zone east of UTC a wall time from before the last transition still compares greater than
it, and the clamp then applies the post-transition offset — an hour out, in roughly 90 zones.
`Asia/Anadyr` at `2011-03-27 02:30` with `nonexistent="shift_backward"` is a clean
example. It needs a walk-back to the last delta whose own UTC value falls at or after its
transition.

**(5) The reverse direction.** `Localizer.utc_val_to_local_val` does an unchecked
`utc_val + delta`, so converting a boundary UTC instant to wall time wraps by 585 years.
This one is not just a bad repr: `tz_localize(None)` and `floor`/`ceil`/`round` store the
wrapped value, and `.year` / `.strftime` agree with it. The scalar path already refuses
the same value via `conversion.check_overflows`, so scalar and array disagree.

I prototyped (5). Notes below, since the fix is less obvious than it looks.

*The wrap is universal, the sentinel is not.* A wrapped local value renders as a wildly wrong
wall time, so it is wrong for every consumer and belongs in the shift. A local value landing
*exactly on* the sentinel still renders the correct wall time through
`pandas_datetime_to_datetimestruct`, and is only unusable once stored into an i8 buffer where
`iNaT` means `NaT`. Rejecting both in the shift regresses consumers that are correct today,
including a test added by GH-66520. For

```python
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp(iNaT + 3600 * 10**9, tz="UTC")]).tz_convert(
    timezone(timedelta(hours=-1))
)   # UTC value representable, local value == iNaT
```

| consumer | today | sentinel rejected in the shift |
|---|---|---|
| `tz_localize(None)` | `NaT`, silent loss | raises ✔ |
| `.year` / `.month` | `-1`, silently wrong | raises ✔ |
| `to_period("ns")` | `NaT`, silent loss | raises ✔ |
| `to_pydatetime()` | `1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224` ✔ | regressed |
| `to_period("D")`, `astype(object)`, `.resolution`, `.is_normalized` | correct ✔ | regressed |
| `read_csv` on `1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224192-01:00` | parses ✔ | regressed — breaks `test_parse_dates_c_fastpath_nat_sentinel_shifts_into_range` |

So: checked add in the shift, sentinel rejected by the consumers that *store* it. There are
exactly two — `tz_convert_from_utc` (backs `tz_localize(None)` and everything reached via
`_local_timestamps()`), and `dt64arr_to_periodarr` at `freq="ns"` only, where the period
ordinal *is* the local i8 value. `normalize_i8_timestamps` needs nothing: local midnight can
never equal `INT64_MIN`, since `INT64_MIN % ppd != 0`.

*`is_date_array_normalized` has to change in the same commit.* It is the only `Localizer`
loop that does not skip `NPY_NAT` before shifting, so guarding the shift makes
`DatetimeIndex([NaT], tz=<negative offset>).is_normalized` raise. It needs
`if utc_val == NPY_NAT: return False`; a bare `continue` flips all-NaT arrays to `True`.
That is behaviour-preserving — across 597 pytz zones (335 distinct UTC offsets) at
`s`/`ms`/`us`/`ns`, no offset makes `(iNaT + delta) % ppd == 0`. On the DST path today it is
not defined at all: `pos == -1`, so `deltas[-1]` is an out-of-bounds read, a third instance
of (4). Nothing currently tests `is_normalized` with `NaT`.

*The message needs the target tz.* Going UTC→local the only value left to render is the
in-bounds UTC instant, so `raise_out_of_bounds` reads as nonsense — `Converting 1677-09-21
00:12:43 underflows past 1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224193`, where the named value looks fine.
An optional `to_tz` argument fixes it. The sentinel case does not need one; there the
rendered value *is* the offending local wall time.

*Cost.* The checked add is ~0.8 ns/element. As a `Localizer` method, so `tz` and `_creso`
ride along in `self`, that is +4–6% on `tz_convert_from_utc` over 1M values; as a
module-level helper taking a `tzinfo` argument it is +29% on the fixed-offset path, so the
argument passing dominates rather than the check.

*Test notes.* Zones per leg: `Asia/Tokyo` and `Pacific/Kiritimati` for the DST bisect (both
`has_tz_rule=False` — `Asia/Tokyo` is the trap, it does *not* take the fastpath),
`Europe/Berlin` + `Timestamp.max` for the zoneinfo `has_tz_rule` fastpath (transition
generation stops at 2100, so `max` lands past `last_trans`), `Etc/GMT±5` for fixed offset,
and `tm.set_timezone` + `dateutil.tz.tzlocal()` for tzlocal. Tests have to materialize:
`DatetimeIndex.tz_convert` is lazy, and so is `DatetimeIndex([<int>], tz=...)`.
`Timestamp(<int>, tz=...)` is eager, and is the most direct user-visible form of (5).
`Timestamp.replace` is not reachable — construction raises first.

### Expected Behavior

A computed `datetime64` value equal to `NPY_NAT` is unrepresentable and should raise
`OutOfBoundsDatetime`, exactly like a value one unit further out already does — not "this
is a nonexistent time", not `NaT`, not a wrapped value. `NPY_NAT + 1` (`Timestamp.min`)
must keep working, and genuine ambiguous/nonexistent handling and `NaT` passthrough must
be untouched.

```python
pd.Timestamp("1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224192").tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo")
# OutOfBoundsDatetime: Converting 1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224192 underflows past
# 1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224193

# one nanosecond later shifts to Timestamp.min and is fine
pd.Timestamp("1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224193").tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo")
# Timestamp('1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224193+091859', tz='Asia/Tokyo')
```

### Issue Description

There are three python api call patterns that ujson objToJson doesn't reliably check the result code for:
 - Converting unicode to utf8. (for example "\ud800" can fail)
 - Converting very large integers to string
 - Calling Various dunder methods that usually behave predicably.

I came into this via some fuzz testing I was doing, which found this:

```
ujson.ujson_dumps({1 << 1_000_000: "value"})
```

But then a review of the `objToJSON` with the help of codex came up with the following inputs that cause ujson to segfault:
 - decimal.Decimal subclasses with a `__format__` method that returns a lone surrogate
 - `datetime.time` subclasses whose `isoformat()` return a non-string, or lone surrogate value
 - `__dir__` methods on objects that raise
 - `__dir__` methods on objects that return a lone surrogate value.
 - Set() subclasses whose `__iter__` raises
 - encoding int values whose string representation > `sys.get_int_max_str_digits()` digits long
 - `dict` keys that are lone surrogate values
 - `dict` keys that are `int` values that are too long
 - `dict` keys that are are objects whose `__str__()` method returns a lone surrogate.
 - 'labels' arrays with invalid surrogate values

All of these are unusual/obscure cases, and apart from the massive int case, are not exercisable just by processing 'untrusted' data.

The fixes here are just to check the respective python api calls and handle them appropriately.

DEPR: Using lists and tuples interchangeably in resample

Ref: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65807#discussion_r3383822680

```python
dti = pd.date_range(start=datetime(2005, 1, 1), end=datetime(2005, 1, 10), freq="Min")
test_series = pd.Series(np.random.default_rng(2).random(len(dti)), dti)
test_frame = pd.DataFrame({"A": test_series, "B": test_series, "C": np.arange(len(dti))})
r = test_frame.resample("h")["A", "B"]
```

The value passed to `__getitem__` on the last line here is `("A", "B")`, which is currently being treated the same way a list would in

    r = test_frame.resample("h")[["A", "B"]]

This should instead be treated as accessing a MultiIndex with levels `"A"` and `"B"` (which does not exist here, raising a KeyError instead).

BUG: assert_series_equal ignores atol/rtol when comparing integer and float dtypes with check_dtype=False

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

left = pd.Series([2**60 + 1], dtype="int64")
right = pd.Series([float(2**60)], dtype="float64")  # exactly 2**60, so the two values are 1 apart

pd.testing.assert_series_equal(
    left, right, check_dtype=False, check_exact=False, rtol=0, atol=0.5
)
# no AssertionError, even though the values are 1 apart and atol is 0.5
```

### Issue Description

With `check_dtype=False` and `check_exact=False`, comparing an integer Series against a float Series ignores `atol` and `rtol` completely.

`assert_almost_equal` short-circuits on [`array_equivalent`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/44ae06694d/pandas/_libs/testing.pyx#L139-L140) before any tolerance logic runs. `array_equivalent` casts the two arrays to a common dtype, so `2**60 + 1` becomes `float(2**60)`, the arrays compare equal, and the elementwise comparison that would apply `rtol`/`atol` is never reached.

The same thing happens with the nullable dtypes (`Int64` vs `Float64`), and through `assert_frame_equal` and `assert_index_equal`.

This is the same symptom as #66400 but a different code path. #66400 was the `double` cast inside `assert_almost_equal` itself, which is fixed in #66696; this one happens earlier, before that code is reached, so it is not covered by that PR.

Worth noting that `array_equivalent` also backs `Index.equals` and `DataFrame.equals`, where casting to a common dtype is reasonable, so a fix likely needs to be scoped to the testing path rather than changing `array_equivalent` itself.

### Expected Behavior

`atol=0.5` should not accept two values that are 1 apart. The tolerance should be applied to the actual values.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on main at commit 44ae06694d.

</details>

#### Code Sample

```python
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2] * 3,
...                    'b': [True, False] * 3,
...                    'c': [1.0, 2.0] * 3})
>>> df.select_dtypes(include=None)
ValueError: at least one of include or exclude must be nonempty
>>> df.select_dtypes(include=[None])
        c

2       1.0
3       2.0
4       1.0
5       2.0
```

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> np.dtype(None)
dtype('float64')
```

#### Problem description

Currently the method deals with regular `None` arguments by turning them into empty tuples:
```python
if not is_list_like(include):
            include = (include,) if include is not None else ()
if not is_list_like(exclude):
            exclude = (exclude,) if exclude is not None else ()
```

BLD: Cython 3.3.0 breaks the from-source CI builds with -Werror=array-bounds

### Installation check

- [X] I have read the [installation guide](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/getting_started/install.html#installing-pandas).

### Platform

manylinux_2_28_i686, Alpine musl, and ubuntu-24.04 with Python 3.15.0rc1, all on CI

### Installation Method

Building from source

### pandas Version

main

### Python Version

3.13 and 3.15.0rc1

### Installation Logs

<details>

Three CI jobs on `main` stopped building yesterday:

- `Linux-32-bit`
- `Linux-Musl`
- `python-dev (ubuntu-24.04)`

All three die the same way, while compiling the Cython generated C, so `pip` never
gets past metadata generation and no tests run:

```
pandas/_libs/tslibs/tzconversion.cpython-313-i386-linux-gnu.so.p/tzconversion.pyx.c:23422:22:
error: array subscript 16 is outside array bounds of 'PyObject[1]' {aka 'struct _object[1]'} [-Werror=array-bounds=]

/opt/_internal/cpython-3.13.15/include/python3.13/object.h:349:34:
error: array subscript 'PyVarObject[0]' is partly outside array bounds of 'PyObject[1]' {aka 'struct _object[1]'} [-Werror=array-bounds=]

ninja: build stopped: subcommand failed.
error: metadata-generation-failed
```

</details>

### Cause

This looks like the Cython 3.3.0 release rather than anything in pandas.

Timeline on `main`:

| commit | date (UTC) | these three jobs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bcd74fb154fc` | 2026-08-21 21:18 | green |
| `1026aa1ba6d0` | 2026-08-22 15:18 | red |

Only two commits sit between those, [`eb5466f1`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/commit/eb5466f1be4e) (CLN, json test coverage) and [`1026aa1b`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/commit/1026aa1ba6d0) (DEPR, CachedAccessor). Both are pure Python and neither touches `tzconversion.pyx` or any C.

Cython 3.3.0 was uploaded to PyPI on 2026-08-22 at 05:16 UTC, which falls between
the last green build and the first red one. The failing jobs confirm they picked it
up:

```
Cython compiler for the host machine: cython (cython 3.3.0)
```

They are entitled to, since `pyproject.toml` currently asks for `Cython>3.1.0,<4`.
The jobs that break are the ones that build from source with `-Werror` under GCC 14,
which is why the wheel based jobs are unaffected.

The compile line already suppresses four warning families but not this one:

```
-Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wno-overflow -Wno-type-limits -Wno-shift-count-overflow -Wno-sign-compare
```

### Possible fixes

I did not want to guess which of these you would prefer, so I am reporting rather
than opening a PR:

1. Add `-Wno-array-bounds` to the existing suppression list, which matches how the
   other Cython generated warnings are already handled.
2. Cap the build requirement at `Cython>3.1.0,<3.3` until the generated code is
   clean, and sync `environment.yml` and `asv.conf.json` with it.
3. Report it upstream to Cython, if the generated indexing is genuinely out of
   bounds rather than GCC being conservative about the `PyObject` to `PyVarObject`
   casts.

Happy to put up a PR for whichever you would like, though I cannot build 32 bit or
musl locally to verify it, so it would need a CI run to confirm.

Related: #63701 re-enabled `-Werror` on CI, and #46360 tracks an older 32 bit
`-Werror` failure with a different warning.

As an explanation what is going on here:

If low memory is True, the file is read in chunks. Unfortunately every chunk determines the number of columns for itself. One of your chunks starts with 15 columns, hence the error when it encounters 23.

One workaround (if you know the number of columns) is to set the names attribute. This forces 23 as expected columns and does not raise an error.

I think the problem is obvious - you're running out of memory because you're trying to load so much data into memory at once, and then process it.

You need to either:

- get a machine with more memory.
- re-architect the solution to use a pipelined approach using either a generator or coroutine pipeline to do the processing stepwise over your data.

The problem with the first approach is it won't scale indefinitely and is expensive. The second way is the right way to do it, but needs more coding.

Also, the pandas.parser.CParserError: [Error tokenizing data](http://net-informations.com/ds/err/token.htm) generated when reading a file written by pandas.to_csv(), it might be because there is a carriage return ('\r') in a column names, in which case to_csv() will actually write the subsequent column names into the first column of the data frame, it will cause a difference between the number of columns in the first X rows. This difference is one cause of the CParserError .

This has nothing to do with memory issues. This is an implementation bug occurring when reading in chunks

BUG: TextFileReader uses an incorrect encoding to test the size of the separator

### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
# Run in UTF-8 mode (`python -X utf8 reproducible_example.py`) just in case.

import pandas as pd
import tempfile

with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("wt", encoding="latin-1") as f:
    f.write("key\u00A5value\ntables\u00A5rectangular")
    f.seek(0)
    pd.read_csv(f.name, sep="\u00A5", encoding="latin-1")
```


### Issue Description

Despite the fact that the encoding of the file to be read is clearly specified as `"latin-1"` (ISO 8859-1), which encodes U+00A5 ¥ YEN SIGN as a single octet, `read_csv` raises the following warning:

```
.../venv/lib/python3.9/site-packages/pandas/util/_decorators.py:311: ParserWarning: Falling back to the 'python' engine because the separator encoded in utf-8 is > 1 char long, and the 'c' engine does not support such separators; you can avoid this warning by specifying engine='python'.
  return func(*args, **kwargs)
```

The cause of this bug is that [`TextFileReader` erroneously uses `sys.getfilesystemencoding()` to determine the encoding](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/v1.4.1/pandas/io/parsers/readers.py#L1056). Even as a default, this would be incorrect: the filesystem encoding is about file names, not about file contents.

This bug has been present [from the commit that initially added this warning](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/commit/5db52f0d3000cb78322ffb148b3f94b3c883bb26#diff-d1a3522340dfa3acb1fa6c5aee6c0e607d018a52b66625e7572b5bcad92e2f6cR786).

BUG: read_excel(engine="odf") ignores office:value on <table:covered-table-cell>

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from odf.opendocument import OpenDocumentSpreadsheet
from odf.table import CoveredTableCell, Table, TableCell, TableRow

path = Path("covered_cell_value.ods")

doc = OpenDocumentSpreadsheet()
sheet = Table(name="Sheet1")
doc.spreadsheet.addElement(sheet)

row0 = TableRow()
sheet.addElement(row0)
row0.addElement(TableCell(valuetype="float", value="1"))
row0.addElement(TableCell(valuetype="float", value="100"))

# A covered cell carrying its own explicit office:value/office:value-type —
# this is exactly what the cells covered by an ODF array/matrix formula
# (table:number-matrix-rows-spanned) hold, per the OpenDocument spec.
row1 = TableRow()
sheet.addElement(row1)
row1.addElement(CoveredTableCell(valuetype="float", value="42"))
row1.addElement(TableCell(valuetype="float", value="200"))

doc.save(str(path))

print(pd.read_excel(path, engine="odf", header=None))
print(pd.read_excel(path, engine="calamine", header=None))


Output:


     0    1
0  1.0  100
1  NaN  200      # engine="odf": the covered cell's value (42) is silently dropped

    0    1
0   1  100
1  42  200       # engine="calamine": reads the same file correctly


(LibreOffice shows correctly the number 42 when opening the file manually.)
```

### Issue Description

`read_excel(engine="odf")` treats every `<table:covered-table-cell>` as empty,
without ever inspecting whether it carries its own `office:value`/
`office:value-type`. The relevant code, in
`pandas/io/excel/_odfreader.py`, `ODFReader.get_sheet_data`:

```python
if sheet_cell.qname == table_cell_name:
    value = self._get_cell_value(sheet_cell)
else:
    value = self.empty_value
```

Any cell that isn't literally a `<table:table-cell>` — i.e. any
`<table:covered-table-cell>` — takes the `else` branch and is hard-coded to
`self.empty_value`, regardless of its actual attributes.

This is usually harmless, since a covered cell is normally just a
merged-away placeholder for an ordinary row/column span with no value of its
own. But it's incorrect for the cells covered by an ODF **array/matrix
formula** (`table:number-matrix-rows-spanned` /
`table:number-matrix-columns-spanned`, [OpenDocument v1.2 Part 1, §9.1.5
`<table:covered-table-cell>`](https://docs.oasis-open.org/office/v1.2/os/OpenDocument-v1.2-os-part1.html#__RefHeading__1415592_253892949);
the attribute itself is defined in §19.680, cross-referenced e.g. in
[MS-OODF3](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/office_standards/ms-oodf3/b8bed28a-0722-4814-9e7d-2611229f5eee)):
per the OpenDocument spec, those covered cells hold their own evaluated
result, and real spreadsheet applications (verified with LibreOffice:
`soffice --headless --convert-to csv` recomputes and exports the correct
distinct value for each covered cell) read/recompute them accordingly.

I've confirmed the data is genuinely present and correctly parsed at the
odfpy layer (which pandas' odf engine is built on) — reading the same file

BUG: coerce empty-string IEEE NaN to null for pyarrow floats

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
"""最简复现：CSV 空字段 + double[pyarrow] + 生产赋值，fillna(0) 填不上。"""

from io import StringIO

import pandas as pd

csv = """id,A,B,C
1,1.5,x,1
2,,x,2
3,2.0,x,3
"""

df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv), dtype={"A": "double[pyarrow]"}, keep_default_na=False,
                 na_values=[""])
df = df[["A", "B", "C"]]
df["A"] = df["A"].fillna(0)
print(df)
print("isna:", pd.isna(df["A"]).tolist())
```

### Issue Description

Bug in Arrow float conversion: empty strings become IEEE NaN, so fillna does not fill them

When converting string data (e.g. CSV empty fields ,,) to a floating PyArrow dtype, empty strings are not NA (pd.isna("") is False). to_numeric turns them into IEEE NaN, and _from_sequence_of_strings builds pa.array(..., mask=isna(strings)) with that mask all-False. The NaN is stored as a value (null_count=0), not a pyarrow null.

Default pandas 3 semantics treat NaN as NA (is_nan_na() is True), but isna / fillna only look at is_null(). Result: fillna(0) is a no-op.

### Expected Behavior

Empty CSV fields converted to double[pyarrow] should be pyarrow null (<NA>). isna() is True for those rows, and fillna(0) replaces them with 0.0.

query:
BUG: remaining NaT-sentinel and out-of-bounds gaps in datetimelike arithmetic (GH-66510 follow-ups)

Follow-ups found while fixing GH-66510 for the vectorized offset paths. Each is pre-existing on
`main` (verified at `082e7739`) and out of scope for that PR, but they are the same family of bug:
arithmetic on the raw int64 datetime64 values either lands on the `NaT` sentinel or leaves the
representable range without being reported as such.

Filing as one issue because (1) and (2) each need their two halves fixed together, and the whole
set shares a root cause. Happy to split if that's easier to triage.

### 1. Adding a timedelta can silently produce `NaT`

`NPY_NAT` is `INT64_MIN`, so a result that lands exactly there is indistinguishable from `NaT`
downstream. `add_overflowsafe` checks for int64 overflow but not for this, and the scalar
`_Timestamp.__add__` does not check either:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp.min + pd.Timedelta(-1, "ns")
NaT
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.min]) + pd.Timedelta(-1, "ns")
DatetimeIndex(['NaT'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)
>>> pd.TimedeltaIndex([pd.Timedelta.min]) - pd.Timedelta(1, "ns")
TimedeltaIndex(['NaT'], dtype='timedelta64[ns]', freq=None)
>>> pd.PeriodIndex([pd.Period(ordinal=-2**63 + 1, freq="D")]) - 1
PeriodIndex(['NaT'], dtype='period[D]')
```

All four should raise `OutOfBoundsDatetime` / `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`. Both the scalar and the
array side need to change together — fixing only one would replace this with a scalar/array
disagreement.

### 2. Out-of-bounds month and quarter shifts raise `OverflowError` from the vendored C

`shift_months`, `shift_quarters` and `SemiMonthOffset._apply_array` build their results with
`npy_datetimestruct_to_datetime`, whose overflow check surfaces as a bare `OverflowError` naming
a C source line, where the scalar path raises `OutOfBoundsDatetime`:

```python
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.max]) + pd.DateOffset(months=1)
OverflowError: Overflow occurred at .../pandas/_libs/src/vendored/numpy/datetime/np_datetime.c:512
>>> pd.Timestamp.max + pd.DateOffset(months=1)
OutOfBoundsDatetime: Cannot cast 2262-05-11 23:47:16.854775 to unit='ns' without overflow.
```

Same for `MonthEnd`, `QuarterEnd`, `SemiMonthEnd`, `YearEnd`.

Relatedly, because the month shift is materialized before the timedelta component is applied, a
composed offset whose *final* result is representable is rejected on the array path:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp.max + pd.DateOffset(months=1, days=-31)
Timestamp('2262-04-10 23:47:16.854775807')
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.max]) + pd.DateOffset(months=1, days=-31)
OverflowError: Overflow occurred at .../np_datetime.c:512
```

Fixing that means applying the two components in one pass so the out-of-range intermediate is
never stored.

### 3. `SemiMonthOffset` and `shift_quarters` truncate `n` to 32 bits

`n` is held in a C `int`, so a multiple of `2**32` silently becomes a no-op:

```python
>>> dr = pd.date_range("2000-01-03", periods=1, unit="s")
>>> dr + pd.offsets.SemiMonthEnd(2**32)
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-15'], dtype='datetime64[s]', freq=None)   # == SemiMonthEnd(0)
>>> dr + pd.offsets.QuarterEnd(2**32)
DatetimeIndex(['2000-03-31'], dtype='datetime64[s]', freq=None)   # == QuarterEnd(0)
```

`BusinessDay` and `Week` had the same bug; widening those to `int64_t` is what the GH-66510
follow-up PR does, and the same treatment applies here.

### 4. `ccalendar` truncates years above `2**31`

`dayofweek(int y, int m, int d)`, `year_add_months` and `month_add_months` take the year as a C
`int`, but `npy_datetimestruct.year` is `int64_t`. Reachable only at second resolution, where the
representable range runs to year ~2.9e11:

```python
>>> big = pd.DatetimeIndex(np.array([np.iinfo(np.int64).max], dtype="M8[s]"))
>>> big[0]
Timestamp('292277026596-12-04 15:30:07')
>>> big + pd.DateOffset(months=1)
DatetimeIndex(['219250469-01-04 15:30:07'], dtype='datetime64[s]', freq=None)   # wrapped
>>> big[0].weekday()
OverflowError: value too large to convert to int
```

The weekday truncation also silently gives `BusinessDay` the wrong anchor for such dates, rather
than raising.

### 5. Minor: duplicated `checked_*` externs

`portable.h`'s `checked_add` / `checked_sub` / `checked_mul` are declared in a `cdef extern` block
in `tzconversion.pyx` and again in `offsets.pyx`, with different signatures (`int` vs `bint`, with
and without `noexcept nogil`). Worth hoisting into a shared `.pxd` so they cannot drift.

### Installed versions

`main` @ `082e7739` (3.1.0.dev0)

BUG: str.split returns string formatted list in version 3.0.x

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
# Using the example inhttps://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.str.split.html

s = pd.Series(
    [
        "this is a regular sentence",
        "https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/index.html",
        np.nan,
    ]
)
result=s.astype('category').str.split()
result
```

### Issue Description

Using a slightly modified example in [str.split documentation](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.str.split.html)

The expected `result` should have an object type, which is indeed the case in pandas version 2.3.1. 
Yet in pandas 3.0/3.0.3/3.0.4, the `result` would have `str` type. `result.iloc[0]` would give: `"['this', 'is', 'a', 'regular', 'sentence']"`


### Expected Behavior

`str.split` returns a list of strings, never a string formatted list of strings

### Installed Versions

3.0/3.0.3/3.0.4 have this problem
2.3.1 is fine

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

**Note**: Please read [this guide](https://matthewrocklin.com/blog/work/2018/02/28/minimal-bug-reports) detailing how to provide the necessary information for us to reproduce your bug.

#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example

```python

# Interpolating "inside" gaps with limit gap size of 3

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

ts_index = pd.date_range('2016-01-01','2016-01-2',freq='H')
limit_gap_size = 3

df = pd.DataFrame(index=ts_index, data={'raw':np.random.uniform(size=ts_index.size)})

df.iloc[0:3] = np.nan
df.iloc[5:7] = np.nan
df.iloc[10:16] = np.nan
df.iloc[17:20] = np.nan
df.iloc[23:25] = np.nan

df['filled'] = df.interpolate(limit=limit_gap_size,limit_area='inside')

# solution to specific case
# credit functions below: https://stackoverflow.com/a/54512613/752092
def bfill_nan(arr):
    """ Backward-fill NaNs """
    mask = np.isnan(arr)
    idx = np.where(~mask, np.arange(mask.shape[0]), mask.shape[0]-1)
    idx = np.minimum.accumulate(idx[::-1], axis=0)[::-1]
    out = arr[idx]
    return out

def calc_mask(arr, maxgap):
    """ Mask NaN gaps longer than `maxgap` """
    isnan = np.isnan(arr)
    cumsum = np.cumsum(isnan).astype('float')
    diff = np.zeros_like(arr)
    diff[~isnan] = np.diff(cumsum[~isnan], prepend=0)
    diff[isnan] = np.nan
    diff = bfill_nan(diff)
    return (diff <= maxgap) | ~isnan # <= instead of < compared to SO answer


df['expected'] = df['raw'].interpolate(limit=3,limit_area='inside').where(calc_mask(df['raw'],limit_gap_size))
```

That is the documented behavior. ``limit=3`` means, that at most three consecutive nans are filled. limit_area inside means, that there have to be valid values before and after the nans

This is very surprising behavior, and I would argue that it should *not* be the default, especially for linear interpolation.

I can see why some might want this behavior for `ffill` and `bfill` methods, but with interpolation it's just wrong. If the gap is too big to be filled, partially interpolating using the value from the other side of the gap is just generating garbage data.

Thus, I would argue, for the non-fill cases, this is a bug, not merely an enhancement.

Example:
```python

series.interpolate(method='linear', limit=2, limit_direction='forward')
```

Additional observation of pandas codebase compatibility with Cython 3.0:

pandas code base was not migrated to new `noexcept` keyword introduced in Cython beta 1. This should not be major problem in general - generated code will check for exception when dedicated return value occurs. But this can be issue mainly for functions returning `void` and `inline` functions because:
1.  `void` function will be checked *everytime* when function is called - this is most affecting `nogil` functions - see https://github.com/cython/cython/pull/5327
2. `inline` function should be more performance critical, hence here I suppose we should avoid all overhead.

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
from pandas.core.nanops import nansem

values = np.array(
    [
        [np.nan, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
        [0.0, np.nan, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
        [0.0, 1.0, np.nan, 3.0, 4.0],

        [False, False, True, False, False],
        [False, False, False, True, False],
        [False, False, False, False, True],
        [True, False, False, False, False],

)

# expected: np.array([np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan])
```

TST: Disallow bare tm.assert_produces_warning

Our tests currently ensure that warnings are triggered whenever appropriate, but to ensure end users get a correct and meaningful warning message, we should also make sure the correct warning message is surfaced whenever we check for a warning.

And so I propose we start enforcing the usage of the `match` argument in all uses of `tm.assert_produces_warning`.

Using the regex `assert_produces_warning\([a-zA-Z]*\)`, I was able to find around 200 bare uses of `assert_produces_warning`, and some of them are checking that warnings are not raised, so this will be an easy task to finish and would be a good way for new contributors to get familiar with the pandas codebase.

If all agree, then we can open a new issue which would have instructions for how to find the bare uses, and maybe we can enforce this using our linter. We could also implement a method `tm.external_warning_produced` similiar to `tm.external_error_raised`, which would be equivalent to using `tm.assert_produces_warning(warning, match=None)`
 
 See also #23922, #30999 and #37261.

BUG: read_csv (c engine) heap buffer overflow on short rows before a wide field

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import io
import pandas as pd

n_cols = 5000
wide = "X" * 100_000
# many rows shorter than n_cols, then one wide field, all in one read buffer
data = "a\n" * 40 + wide + "\n"

df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), header=None, names=[f"c{i}" for i in range(n_cols)])
print(df.shape)                 # (41, 5000) as expected
print(len(df.iloc[40, 0]))      # 99999, but the field is 100000 chars
```

### Issue Description

With the C engine, `read_csv` reserves the token stream once per read buffer for the
worst case that the whole buffer is copied 1:1, and the SIMD/scalar bulk-copy fast paths
in `tokenize_bytes` then write field bytes with no per-copy capacity check. When a row has
fewer fields than expected, `end_line` closes the missing fields by writing a NUL
terminator for each one. Those synthetic terminators take stream space but consume no
input, so a run of short rows eats into the reservation the bulk copies rely on. It is
restored only for the terminators themselves (`make_stream_space(ex_fields - fields)`),
not for the input still waiting to be copied.

So a buffer that holds many short rows followed by a wide field ends up with the stream
smaller than that field, and the bulk copy runs past the end of `self->stream`. Building
with ASAN (`-Db_sanitize=address`) reports a `heap-buffer-overflow` WRITE at the
`memcpy`/`*stream++` in `tokenize_bytes`; without a sanitizer the field is silently
truncated or corrupted as above, and larger inputs crash the interpreter. `names=` is one
easy way in because it makes every data row subject to the short-row padding, but any
source with short rows before a wide field in the same 256 KiB read chunk reaches it.

The bulk-copy paths and the reservation live in
`pandas/_libs/src/parser/tokenizer.cpp` (`tokenize_bytes`, `end_line`).

### Expected Behavior

The frame parses without reading or writing past the stream buffer, and the wide field
comes back intact (`len(df.iloc[40, 0]) == 100000`).

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on the current main branch (commit e0839ed).

</details>

I think the next step is to isolate the stream-space reservation path around `tokenize_bytes` / `end_line` and see whether short-row padding needs to reserve input-carrying space separately from synthetic terminators.

DOC: Add mention that read_csv() returns column indices always as strings

Edit [rhshadrach]: The issue described below is expected behavior from pandas. This issue is to be resolved just by adding documentation to the docstring of read_csv indicating this.

### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

idx = [0,1,2]
df = pd.DataFrame(0,index=idx, columns=idx)
print(df)
df.to_csv("Test.csv")
df2 = pd.read_csv("Test.csv", header=[0], index_col=[0])
print(df2)

#Test.csv   
#All values, including row and column indices, are integers
#,0,1,2
#0,0,0,0
#1,0,0,0
#2,0,0,0

#  row and column indices of original df are integers
print(df.columns)
print(df.index)

# column indices of df created from csv are strings
print(df2.columns)
print(df2.index)

# Work-around:
df_temp = pd.read_csv('Test.csv',header=[0], index_col=[0])
df3 = pd.DataFrame(0,index = df_temp.index, columns=[])
for c in df_temp.columns:
    newc:int = int(c)
    df3[newc] = df_temp[c]
print(df3.columns)
```


### Issue Description

Issue:  read_csv() returns the column indices, created as integers,  as strings rather than integers. However, the row index is returned as integers.   

The programmer assumes the columns are integers because that is how the original df was created, so will get a KeyError when running df[0], when only df['0'] now works. 

FYI, the same problem occurs for MultiIndex dataframes:  df[('0','0') works but df[(0,0)] generates a KeyError.

This is a difficult bug (unexpected feature?) to find because the difference is not evident when printing the dataframe, only when printing df.columns.  The Variable Explorer in Spyder also displays 0 not '0' for the column indices, so I may cross-post this to Spyder.

For database processing, the use of integer column indices is rare, but for those that use the index value as part of the computation, such as X(i+1) = F(X(i)), having integer indices is convenient, if not important.  The main thing is that the recreation of row and column indices from csv files are unexpectedly different.   

I would assume that the same behaviour could be in other file importers.

A suggestions for removing the confusion:
1. Add a parameter in read_csv to select the dtype of the column (and row) index, just as there are parameters to select the dtype of the data in the columns.
2. Add a parameter to to_csv() to specify the dtype of the indices.  This is probably the best solution since it will create csv files that are correctly formated. eg.  strings have quotes around them, while integers do not.  That way read_csv() has a way to interprete the formating.



### Expected Behavior

See Issue Description and run sample code

```python
def _warn_max_colwidth_too_small(key):
```

Well, that's because the `dt` accessor always return a frequency when it's inferrable:

```python
import pandas as pd

date_range = pd.date_range("2020", periods=5, freq="D")
date_range.freq = None  # remove frequency from index

s = pd.Series(data=date_range, index=None)
print(s.dt.freq)  # 'D' - dt infers frequency
```

Freq is still being dropped by tz_localize. It is actually maintained if you use tz_localize via dt:
```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(
    index=pd.date_range("2020", periods=5, freq="D"),
    data=pd.date_range("2020", periods=5, freq="D"),
    name="date"
)
print(s.index.freq)  
print(s.tz_localize("europe/london").index.freq)  
print(s.dt.tz_localize("europe/london").index.freq)
```

Prints:
```
<Day>
None
<Day>
```

However, if you directly work with the index this `dt` is not available, but you can overwrite the freq from the inferred freq property:
```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(
    index=pd.date_range("2020", periods=5, freq="D"),
    data=pd.date_range("2020", periods=5, freq="D"),
    name="date"
)
index = s.index
index_aware = index.tz_localize("europe/london")
print(index.freq)  
print(index_aware.freq)  
index_aware.freq = index_aware.inferred_freq
print(index_aware.freq)  
```

Prints:
```
<Day>
None
<Day>
```

No clue how robust this is, so it would be great if the freq can just be passed when applying `tz_convert`.

BUG: Inconsistent number conversion with leading zeros in to_numeric()

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

int_only = pd.Series([0, 10084566, "10084566", "000000000010084566"])
int_with_float = pd.Series([0, 10084566.0, "10084566", "000000000010084566"])
int_with_missings = pd.Series([pd.NA, 10084566, "10084566", "000000000010084566"])
alnum_mix = pd.Series(["TWZ10084566", 10084566, "10084566", "000000000010084566"])

# works as expected
print("All values non-missing integer values [works]:")
print(pd.to_numeric(int_only))
print()

# inconsistent
print("All values numeric, integer & float mixed [inconsistent]:")
print(pd.to_numeric(int_with_float))
print()

print("All values are integer or missing [inconsistent]:")
print(pd.to_numeric(int_with_missings))
print()

print("Numeric values mixed with non-numeric strings [inconsistent]:")
print(pd.to_numeric(alnum_mix, errors="coerce"))
print()
```

### Issue Description

I was doing a conversion of a mixed object-type pd.Series, integer numbers where stored with leading zeros, some values were missing, some values were alpha-numeric. So, I ran `pd.to_numeric(series, errors="coerce")`

And this is where I encountered an inconsistency in how numbers are converted. As soon as missings, alpha-numeric, or float values are involved, the series in converted to `float64`; otherwise the outcome would be `int64`. `int64` is fine, `float64` apparently has a precision issue with leading zeros und some numbers are rounded.

Specifically, for example: `"000000000010084566"` becomes a different number, depending on the other values in the Series and the determined dtype. If only integers are present it becomes `10084566`, as soon as other values force the Series to become float64, it becomes `10084560.0`. "10084566" converts fine.

### Expected Behavior

`"000000000010084566"` should be converted to `10084566` or `10084566.0` by `pd.to_numeric()`, no matter which other values are present or which dtype the return becomes.

BUG: Series.unstack(sort=False) puts the NaN column first while its values stay in place

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ser = pd.Series(
    [1.0, 2.0, 3.0],
    index=pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(
        [("r", 8.0), ("r", 7.0), ("r", np.nan)], names=["x", "z"]
    ),
)
print(ser.unstack(1, sort=False))
print(ser.to_frame("v").unstack(1, sort=False))
```

### Issue Description

With `sort=False`, `Series.unstack` places the `NaN` column of the unstacked level at position 0,
but the *values* stay at the position where `NaN` first appeared. Every column ends up mislabelled:

```
z  NaN  8.0  7.0
x
r  1.0  2.0  3.0
```

`1.0` belongs to `8.0`, `2.0` to `7.0` and `3.0` to `NaN`, so each value is shifted one column left.
Nothing raises and nothing warns.

`DataFrame.unstack` on the same data is correct, so the two paths disagree:

```
     v
z  8.0  7.0  NaN
x
r  1.0  2.0  3.0
```

The divergence is in `_Unstacker.get_new_columns`: the `value_columns is None` branch (used by
`Series.unstack` with a numpy dtype) does `self.removed_level.insert(0, ...)` unconditionally,
while the `value_columns is not None` branch derives the position from `self._repeater`, which
honours `self.unique_nan_index`. Only the `sort=True` case wants position 0 (that is what
`self.lift` does); with `sort=False` the values are never lifted.

Note an extension-dtype `Series` routes through `_unstack_extension_series` -> `DataFrame.unstack`,
so it takes the correct branch — only the numpy-dtype `Series` path is affected.

### Expected Behavior

`ser.unstack(1, sort=False)` should give columns `[8.0, 7.0, NaN]`, matching the values and matching
`DataFrame.unstack`.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on main at `ff1d39bbdf4` (`3.1.0.dev0+1512.gff1d39bbdf4`). Also present in 2.x.

</details>

ENH: Disclose offending values in `IntervalArray._validate`

### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

When using `IntervalIndex.from_breaks` one ends up at `IntervalArray._validate` which, among others asserts that the left end of the interval is `<=` to the right end.

Yet, it does not disclose the offending values and just raises a generic `left side of interval must be <= right side` `ValueError`. The provided values for the `IntervalArray` may be long so the user may not be able to easily spot the offenders.

### Feature Description

At this point an `Exception` is raised so one can assume the the library has completed its task. Hence a slight overhead for a improved error message may be acceptable. Only challenge is to not overcharge the error message, in case there are many offenders.

One possible solution could be to change

```python
        if not (left[left_mask] <= right[left_mask]).all():
            msg = "left side of interval must be <= right side"
```

to something like (pseudo code)

```python
order_offenders = left[left_mask] > right[left_mask]
if order_offenders.any():
    msg = f"left side of interval must be <= right side. offending intervals: {zip(left[order_offenders], right[order_offenders]}"
```

### Alternative Solutions

Alternatively, if this seems to risky or resource intensive, maybe just printing the first 5 offending indices is already helpful

(pseudocode)

```python
order_offenders = left[left_mask] > right[left_mask]
if order_offenders.any():
    msg = f"left side of interval must be <= right side. offending locations: {order_offenders[order_offenders].index.head(5)}"
```

interval.overlaps() mishandles empty intervals

The special case where `left=right` is not checked properly by the constructor, only `closed='both'` (a point)  or `closed='neither'` (an empty interval) makes sense but '[0,0)' or `(0,0]` are nonsensical. The `overlaps` method returns inconsistent results when encountering such Intervals. 

```python
import pandas as pd
pd.Interval(0,0,'left')
```

**Update:**
Examples (from below):
```python
In [4]:  
   ...: import pandas as pd
   ...: from pandas import Interval
   ...: 
   ...: a=Interval(0,1,'both')
   ...: b=Interval(0,0,'right')
   ...: print(a.overlaps(b))
   ...: b=Interval(0,0,'left')
   ...: print(a.overlaps(b))
True
False
```
hints:
@pilkibun Thanks for the report

> The `overlaps` method returns inconsistent results when encountering such Intervals.

can you give examples?

cc @jschendel if you have thoughts on the expected behavior here. Should we disallow things like `Interval(0, 0, closed='left')`, or should we update the logic downstream (like `.overlaps`) to consider cases like these?

> can you give examples?
```python
In [4]:  
   ...: import pandas as pd
   ...: from pandas import Interval
   ...: 
   ...: a=Interval(0,1,'both')
   ...: b=Interval(0,0,'right')
   ...: print(a.overlaps(b))
   ...: b=Interval(0,0,'left')
   ...: print(a.overlaps(b))
True
False
```
Since the left side and right side of a point interval coincide, it cannot have one side open and side closed at the same time. `overlaps`  returns a different answer based on which "side" of a point we look it, which strikes me as wrong. 

This is a pathological corner case but programmatically you may end up creating such intervals,
in which case allowing this ambiguity could introduce subtle bugs. 

With the PR change pandas will complain loudly to warn the user, and force them to handle the case explicitly as either an empty interval `(x,x)`, or a single point `[x,x]`.

> Should we disallow things like `Interval(0, 0, closed='left')`?

I'm -1 on this, as it would be inconsistent with other interval implementations I've seen, which allow empty intervals.  From what I can tell, other interval implementations tend to fall into two categories:

1. `left == right` is allowed for any `closed` with support for empty intervals.
2. `closed='both'` is only supported, so `left == right` isn't really an issue, but empty intervals are still supported.

Disallowing `left == right` for `closed='left'/'right'` would seem to diverge from other implementations.  It seems like this would also lead to some internal inconsistencies: since `IntervalIndex` and `IntervalArray` require having the same `closed`, this would make empty intervals not supported in `closed='left'/'right'` arrays/indexes, but supported in the `closed='neither'` case with no obvious way to work around (i.e. in the scalar interval case you can just tell people to use  `closed='neither'` but this is not the case for indexes/arrays).

Some examples of other interval implementations:
- Using postgres range types: 
   - `SELECT int8range(0, 0, '(]')` returns `empty`
   - `SELECT int8range(0, -1, '(]')` raises: `Error: range lower bound must be less than or equal to range upper bound`.
- Using octave (open source matlab):
  -  `infsupdec ()` returns `[Empty]_trv`  (I don't think you can specify `closed != 'both'`?)
  - `infsupdec (0, -1)` returns `[NaI]`, along with some warnings (`NaI` = Not an Interval) 

The above does raise a question as to whether or not we want to specifically add a custom `EmptyInterval` object similar to the other implementations above.  Not sure if the additional complexity needed to support this offsets any decrease in ops complexity that having such an object would enable.  I think the only real benefit would be a nicer repr?  Adding an `is_empty` property is another alternative that might be a bit simpler.

Adding `NaI` seems like it'd be way too large of a burden to maintain, and I think the core team would have me killed for suggesting we add yet another NA representation, so that's likely off the table.

> Or should we update the logic downstream (like `.overlaps`) to consider cases like these?

Yes, IMO the downstream logic should handle empty intervals.

> `[0,0)` or `(0,0]` are nonsensical

Not really, from a mathematical perspective these definitions are valid and equivalent to `(0, 0)`: 
- ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5332445/59635190-ceb3c100-910d-11e9-876c-4478c33f5739.png)

Thanks for the writeup @jschendel. FWIW (not much), my intutiton matches yours here.

Also noting https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/26894#pullrequestreview-250742121 here, which belongs as part of the discussion here.

I also just noticed that for postgres `(0,0) == (999,999) == empty`, i.e. empty intervals have no reference point on the line, they are just singletons:

```
postgres=# SELECT int8range(0, 0, '[)') = int8range(42, 42, '()');
 ?column? 
----------
 t
(1 row)

```

That makes me even more skeptical about the logic of having empty intervals included in an index,
for when you chop up an interval into bins for example. For one thing, you could end up with duplicates in your index, which is bad news. for another, having a singleton botches ordering, which means you can't have an ordered index (or you'd have to decide on an arbitary rule) for `searchsorted` to work.

> But in that case, you must agree that nothing should ever overlap with either '(x,x]' or '[x,x)'. And I've already given an example where this is violated.

Yes, of course, but this is a bug in the `overlaps` method. Disallowing `(x, x]` and `[x, x)` won't fix the issue, as it's still present with `(x, x)`:
```python
In [1]: import pandas as pd; pd.__version__
Out[1]: '0.25.0.dev0+750.gbaa77c33f'

In [2]: a = pd.Interval(-1, 1, closed='both')

In [3]: b = pd.Interval(0, 0, closed='neither')

In [4]: a.overlaps(b)
Out[4]: True
```

> So the current implementation clearly does not conform to what you claim as a reference/correct/consistent implementation.

I never said that our implementation was consistent with postgres, or any other implementation.  Ideally we'd conform to the common conventions, but intervals are still relatively new in pandas - there are still many features that need to be added, and corner cases that need to be addressed (as you've discovered here).

My point was disallowing `(x, x]` and `[x, x)` by making them raise takes us further away from common conventions associated with intervals.  It'd be akin `int8range(0, 0, '[)')` and `int8range(0, 0, '(]')` erroring in postgres with `int8range(0, 0, '()')` being allowed.

To be clear, I'm NOT against changing the behavior of how pandas handles `(x, x]` and `[x, x)`, e.g. perhaps creating an `EmptyInterval` object so that `Interval(0, 0, closed='left') == Interval(0, 0, closed='right') == Interval(0, 0, closed='neither') == EmptyInterval()`, provided it's done in a maintainable way.  Having the constructor raise is what I'm against.

I don't think silently converting these to `closed='neither'` would be a clean solution, as my impression is that this would require a bit of special casing to make this fully compatible with a left/right closed `IntervalArray` or `IntervalIndex`.  I haven't gone through the code to attempt doing this though, so perhaps it's not actually too bad.

> For one thing, you could end up with duplicates in your index, which is bad news

Indexes in pandas generically support dupes, so this is something that will be accounted for regardless.

> having a singleton botches ordering, which means you can't have an ordered index (or you'd have to decide on an arbitary rule)

Likewise indexes in pandas generically support missing values, which similarly botch ordering, and will be accounted for regardless.  I'm guessing that empty intervals can handled in a similar manner.

I suppose this could be an argument for maintaining the existing behavior, as the current implementation does not botch ordering.

> Can you can suggest offhand a real-world example where such an interval would be created and it isn't a bug?

This can come about via the contraction of intervals, i.e. restricting intervals so that they lie within a given observation interval, and then using the contracted intervals to scale things where you'd want empty intervals to count as zero.  Admittedly, the machinery to do this idiomatically does not exist in pandas yet, but the methods to do so are things that have been discussed.

This doesn't necessitate using an `IntervalIndex`, and could be done with an `IntervalArray` instead, but a large portion of code is shared between the two, and pandas generally doesn't enforce restrictions on what an index can contain vs. an equivalent array.

DEPR: `groupby.nth.__getitem__`

The `nth` method on groupby can be called in 2 ways

```python
df.groupby(...).nth([0, 1])
df.groupby(...).nth[0, 1]
```

Which both dispatch to the same implementation

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/633e72f17a6e94dd1d350320ab10caf0c25d5300/pandas/core/groupby/indexing.py#L371-L379

In the original issue it was stated the `__getitem__` route is just syntactic sugar, https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/44589.

IMO it would be clearer and simpler if there was one form to call this API, and since `dropna` is an argument, the `__getitem__` implementation should be deprecated

BUG: read_csv with usecols raises IndexError in low-memory mixed-dtype warning path

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import csv
import pandas as pd

file = "repro.csv"

N_COLS = 87
N_ROWS = 20000
TARGET_POS = 50
TARGET_COL = "Overall_Judgment"
SWITCH_ROW = 8192

columns = [f"col_{i}" for i in range(N_COLS)]
columns[TARGET_POS] = TARGET_COL

with open(file, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(columns)

    for i in range(N_ROWS):
        row = ["x"] * N_COLS

        if i < SWITCH_ROW:
            row[TARGET_POS] = "YES"
        else:
            row[TARGET_POS] = ""

        writer.writerow(row)

pd.read_csv(file, usecols=[TARGET_COL])
```

### Issue Description

On pandas 3.0.5, read_csv raises an internal IndexError when usecols selects a
column that is not at position 0 in the original CSV and different low-memory
chunks infer different dtypes for that column.

In the reproducible example above, the selected column contains strings in the
first low-memory chunk and only missing values in later chunks.

The traceback ends with:

    File "pandas/io/parsers/c_parser_wrapper.py", line 361, in _concatenate_chunks
        warning_columns.append(column_names[name])
                               ~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^
    IndexError: list index out of range

Changing only TARGET_POS from 50 to 0 makes the IndexError disappear. In that
case, read_csv succeeds and emits the expected DtypeWarning instead.

The following workarounds also succeed:

- low_memory=False
- explicitly specifying dtype for the selected column
- engine="python"

This suggests that the failure occurs in the low-memory mixed-dtype warning path
when usecols is used for a column whose original position is greater than 0.

### Expected Behavior

read_csv should successfully return the selected column.

If different low-memory chunks cause mixed dtype inference, pandas may emit a
DtypeWarning, as it does when the selected column is at position 0, but it
should not raise an internal IndexError.

TST: assert_frame_equal now raises for mismatching freq in MultiIndex level

We already raised for a mismatching freq for a normal Datetime/TimedeltaIndex in `assert_frame_equal`, and https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65194 updated `assert_index_equal` to have a similar behaviour (behind a deprecation warning first).

But a potential side effect of that PR (didn't verify) is that this now raises for a MultiIndex level:

```python
dates = pd.date_range("2012-01-01", periods=3)
midx1 = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([dates, [1, 2, 3]])
midx2 = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([dates._with_freq(None), [1, 2, 3]])
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}, index=midx1)
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}, index=midx2)
```

On main:

```python
# this now raises a warning -> expected
>>> pd.testing.assert_index_equal(midx1, midx2)
Pandas4Warning: assert_index_equal will check the 'freq' attribute by default in a future version; these freqs <Day> and None do not match. Pass check_freq=True or check_freq=False to silence this warning

# this directly errors
>>> pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(df1, df2)
...
Attribute "freq" are different
[left]:  <Day>
[right]: None
```

while with released pandas (3.0.5) both cases pass:

```python
>>> pd.testing.assert_index_equal(midx1, midx2)
>>> pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(df1, df2)
```

cc @jbrockmendel
hints:
Dug into this a bit — the root cause looks like a default-value mismatch between the two functions:

**assert_index_equal's** check_freq defaults to **lib.no_default**, which is what triggers the "warn instead of raise" deprecation path.

assert_frame_equal, though, defaults check_freq to plain **True**. When it calls assert_index_equal internally, it passes that explicit True down. For a flat DatetimeIndex this doesn't matter (the top-level check still isn't hit the same way), but for a MultiIndex, assert_index_equal recurses per-level and just forwards whatever check_freq it was given — so the explicit True propagates into the per-level check and skips the warn-first sentinel path entirely, hitting the hard **assert_attr_equal("freq", ...)** raise.

So it seems like the fix would be having **assert_frame_equal** pass **lib.no_default** (rather than an explicit True) as the default it forwards to assert_index_equal, to preserve the warn-first behavior consistently.

Thanks @YuktaBansal19 for the investigation on the issue. I reproduced the behavior locally and confirmed that the resolved `check_freq=True` from `assert_frame_equal` was being propagated into `MultiIndex` level comparisons.

I've added a regression test covering the default, `check_freq=True`, and `check_freq=False` cases, and adjusted the index comparison to preserve the existing behavior for non-`MultiIndex` indexes while allowing the unresolved `check_freq` value to propagate through `MultiIndex` levels.

All relevant tests and pre-commit checks are passing.

BUG: `DataFrame.eval` inconsistently handles duplicated columns

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {'a': range(3), 'b': range(10, 13), 'c': range(3)}
).rename(columns={'b': 'a'})

print(df)
print(df.eval('a == 1'))
print(pd.eval('a == 1', resolvers=(df,)))
```

### Issue Description

`Dataframe.eval ` behaves differently from `pandas.eval()` when a `DataFrame` contains duplicated column names.

In the example above, the `DataFrame` has two columns named `a`. Evaluating the expression `a == 1` appears to only evaluate one of the duplicated columns (the second one in this case), and returning a `pandas.Series`

In contrast, `pd.eval( ... )` evaluates both duplicated columns and returns a `DataFrame`. 

Similar to #59950

### Expected Behavior

It would be helpful to clarify whether duplicated column names are intended to be supported in both APIs. 

Possible expected behaviors could include: 
* both methods behaving similarly
* raising an explicit exception when expressions reference duplicated names

I think it would be more natural to align `DataFrame.eval` with `pd.eval(..., resolvers=(df,))`.

When a DataFrame has duplicate column labels, `df["a"]` returns a `DataFrame` containing all columns with that label. So I think `df.eval("a == 1")` should also evaluate both `a` columns, rather than silently selecting one of them. This would be more consistent with pandas' existing indexing semantics.

In other words, I think we can keep the current `pd.eval` behavior and adjust the resolver/name-resolution path used by `DataFrame.eval`. If the maintainers agree with this direction, I would be happy to open a PR.

+class _DuplicateColumnRecorder(dict):
+    """
+    Notes whether a query expression referenced a duplicated column label.
+

`TestApi.allowed_api_dirs` in `pandas/tests/api/test_api.py` lists `"internals"`, and `test_api` compares that list against `dir(pandas.api)`. But `pandas/api/__init__.py` does not import the `internals` submodule, and a submodule only shows up in its parent's `dir()` once something has imported it. So the test passes only when an earlier test in the same process has done that — in practice `pandas/tests/internals/test_api.py`.

Run the directory on its own and it fails:

```
$ pytest pandas/tests/api/test_api.py -p no:randomly
FAILED pandas/tests/api/test_api.py::TestApi::test_api - AssertionError: Iterable are different

Iterable length are different
[left]:  6
[right]: 7
[diff]: ['internals']
```

```python
import pandas as pd
"internals" in dir(pd.api)   # False
import pandas.api.internals
"internals" in dir(pd.api)   # True
```

`pandas/api/internals.py` exists and is tracked; this is purely about whether it has been imported.

Not a CI risk today (CI runs the whole suite), but it makes running that one directory locally look broken, and the test is only green because of what its neighbours happened to do first.

Fix is one of:

1. import `internals` from `pandas/api/__init__.py` — it is public API, so arguably `pd.api.internals` should be reachable off a bare `import pandas`;
2. import it in the test before checking; or

BUG: `pivot_table` with `margins=True` raises KeyError when dict aggfunc doesn't cover every aggregated column

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/development/contributing_environment.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "random1": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
        "random2": [10, 20, 30, 40],
        "type": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
    }
)

# aggfunc only covers "random1"; "random2" is picked up implicitly via `values`
df.pivot_table(index="type", aggfunc={"random1": "mean"}, margins=True)
```

### Issue Description

Raises:

```
KeyError: 'random2'
```

Without `margins=True`, the exact same call works fine and silently excludes `random2` from the result (since it isn't a key in the `aggfunc` dict):

```python
>>> df.pivot_table(index="type", aggfunc={"random1": "mean"})
      random1
type
a         1.5
b         3.5
```

This also reproduces when `values` is passed explicitly and includes a column not covered by the dict:

```python
df.pivot_table(index="type", values=["random1", "random2"], aggfunc={"random1": "mean"}, margins=True)
```

The root cause seems to be in `_compute_grand_margin` in `pandas/core/reshape/pivot.py`: it iterates over every column in `data[values]` and looks up `aggfunc[k]` for each one. When `aggfunc` is a dict that doesn't have a key for `k`, this will raise a `KeyError`, which propagates uncaught (only `TypeError` is currently swallowed there). I guess the fix is to skip columns not present in the dict, consistent with the non-margins aggregation path's existing (if implicit) behavior of silently dropping such columns.

I found as an incidental, separate issue while investigating and trying to fix #12210 on my own (dict `aggfunc` containing a list of functions per column + `margins=True`). However, this is a distinct root cause/code path and reproduces independently of list-vs-scalar functions.

### Expected Behavior

`margins=True` should produce the same set of columns as `margins=False` (i.e. silently drop columns the `aggfunc` dict doesn't cover), rather than raising `KeyError`.

### Installed Versions

main branch (post `84d7518bdc`)

BUG: boolean-mask operations on a null-dtype ArrowDtype column abort the process (SIGABRT)

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

ser = pd.Series(pa.array([None, None, None], type=pa.null()), dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.null()))

ser[np.array([True, False, False])] = None   # <- process aborts (SIGABRT)
```

Every one of these aborts the interpreter, all through `ArrowExtensionArray._replace_with_mask`:

```python
ser[np.array([True, False, False])] = None      # boolean-mask setitem
ser.where(np.array([True, False, False]))
ser.mask(np.array([True, False, False]))
ser.combine_first(ser)

df = ser.to_frame("a")
df.loc[np.array([True, False, False]), "a"] = None
```

### Issue Description

For a `null`-typed `ArrowDtype` column, any operation routed through
`ArrowExtensionArray._replace_with_mask` kills the process rather than raising:

```
/arrow/cpp/src/arrow/result.cc:27: Constructed with a non-error status: OK
[1]    79074 abort      python
```

This is a hard abort, not a Python exception, so it cannot be caught and takes down the
interpreter (including a pytest run). It is specific to the `null` type — I swept
`string`, `dictionary`, `int64`, `list`, `struct` and `map` through the same
boolean-mask setitem and all behave correctly.

The root cause is the pyarrow kernel, reduced to:

```python
import pyarrow as pa, pyarrow.compute as pc
pc.replace_with_mask(pa.array([None], pa.null()), [True], pa.scalar(None, type=pa.null()))
```

That was reported upstream as https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/47447 and **is fixed,
but the fix is milestoned for pyarrow 25.0.0**. pandas supports pyarrow >= 13.0.0, so with
every released pyarrow this is currently reachable from public pandas APIs.

`_replace_with_mask` already carries a version-independent workaround for the sibling
`replace_with_mask` defect on chunked booleans, immediately above the failing call:

```python
if isinstance(values, pa.ChunkedArray) and pa.types.is_boolean(values.type):
    # GH#52059 replace_with_mask segfaults for chunked array
    # https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/34634
    values = values.combine_chunks()
try:
    return pc.replace_with_mask(values, mask, replacements)
```

so a guard for the null type would sit naturally next to it — an all-null array has nothing
to mask out, so it can simply be returned unchanged. Alternatively it could be gated on the
existing `pa_version_under25p0` flag, which `array.py` already uses for a different pyarrow 25
behavior change.

Noticed while working on GH-64320; the same helper is called from the fix there.

### Expected Behavior

The operations above should return a `null`-dtype result rather than aborting:

```python
>>> ser[np.array([True, False, False])] = None
>>> ser.tolist()
[<NA>, <NA>, <NA>]
```

At minimum pandas should never abort the interpreter for a supported dtype and a documented
API call.

### Installed Versions

<details>

```
commit                : ebd40365c94b2d34ce56ff5bfe1a527ed1bb7f49
python                : 3.13.11
python-bits           : 64
OS                    : Darwin
pandas                : 3.1.0.dev0+1520.gebd40365c94
numpy                 : 2.4.4
dateutil              : 2.9.0.post0
pyarrow               : 23.0.1
pytz                  : 2026.1.post1
```

</details>

ENH: include cell location in ExcelWriter warning for values exceeding the 32,767 character limit

### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

The `ExcelWriter._value_with_fmt` method checks whether a cell value exceeds Excel's 32,767-character limit and currently raises the following warning:

`UserWarning: Cell contents too long (<cell value length>), truncated to 32767 characters`

The current warning message does not identify which cell contains the truncated value. As a result, users need to further inspect the DataFrame separately to determine which value(s) exceeded the limit.

It would be useful for the warning to include the destination cell location. Here is the expected warning message:

`UserWarning: Cell contents too long (<cell value length>) at row <row>, column <column>; truncated to 32767 characters`

That message makes the warning directly actionable and make it easier to identify truncated values during Excel export.

### Feature Description

Change the  input parameter `val` of the method `ExcelWriter._value_with_fmt` into the **ExcelCell** instance of `cell`. Further update the method to the following format:

```
def _value_with_fmt(
        self, cell: ExcelCell
    ) -> tuple[
        int | float | bool | str | datetime.datetime | datetime.date, str | None
    ]:
        """
        Convert numpy types to Python types for the Excel writers.

        Parameters
        ----------
        cell : ExcelCell
            Spreadsheet cell data that contains the value to be written into cells

        Returns
        -------
        Tuple with the first element being the converted value and the second
            being an optional format
        """
        fmt = None

        val = cell.val
        if is_integer(val):
            val = int(val)
        elif is_float(val):
            val = float(val)
        elif is_bool(val):
            val = bool(val)
        elif is_decimal(val):
            val = Decimal(val)
        elif isinstance(val, datetime.datetime):
            fmt = self._datetime_format
        elif isinstance(val, datetime.date):
            fmt = self._date_format
        elif isinstance(val, datetime.timedelta):
            val = val.total_seconds() / 86400
            fmt = "0"
        else:
            val = str(val)
            # GH#56954
            # Excel's limitation on cell contents is 32767 characters
            # xref https://support.microsoft.com/en-au/office/excel-specifications-and-limits-1672b34d-7043-467e-8e27-269d656771c3
            if len(val) > 32767:
                warnings.warn(
                    f"Cell contents too long ({len(val)}) in row {cell.row}, column {cell.col};"
                    "truncated to 32767 characters",
                    UserWarning,
                    stacklevel=find_stack_level(),
                )
        return val, fmt
```

Update the **four active** function dependency from `cell.val` to only `cell`.

- `def _make_table_cell(...)` on pandas/io/excel/_odswriter.py
- `def _write_cells_write_only(...)` on pandas/io/excel/_openpyxl.py
- `def _write_cells_normal(...)` on pandas/io/excel/_openpyxl.py
- `def _write_cells(...)` on pandas/io/excel/_xlsxwriter.py


### Alternative Solutions

Users can pre-scan the DataFrame for values exceeding 32,767 characters, but this requires an additional investigation of the data. There is currently no built-in way to obtain the location of the truncated cell from the warning itself.

### Additional Context

_No response_
